articles.title_orig: China urges dialogue, political settlement to Middle East conflict
articles.title_zh: China urges dialogue, political settlement to Middle East conflict
articles.content_orig:
China's top diplomat Wang Yi urged all parties to seek a political settlement to the conflict in the Middle East through dialogue and negotiations on Monday, calling for a rational and pragmatic approach to avoid renewed hostilities.
Wang, director of the Office of the Central Commission for Foreign Affairs, made the remarks during a meeting in Beijing with Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council.
As fighting in the Middle East drags on and its spillover effects spread, dialogue and negotiations offer the way forward, Wang said.
He called on all parties to act with a sense of responsibility to their people and to history, meet each other halfway, and focus on a political solution rather than resort to arms again.
China stands ready to work with all parties to continue efforts to restore regional peace, guided by its initiatives and proposals for easing tensions in the Middle East, he said.
Briefing Wang on Iran's views concerning the regional situation, Bagheri Kani said his country would firmly safeguard its security, sovereignty, and territorial integrity, and resist power politics and threats.
Iran is also willing to engage in talks and negotiations with all parties and work actively for regional peace and stability, he said.
He expressed appreciation for China's initiatives and proposals and its consistent commitment to multilateralism, saying Iran looks forward to China playing a greater role in international and regional peace.
On bilateral ties, Wang said China-Iran relations have maintained steady development despite a volatile international landscape. This serves the fundamental interests of both peoples and reflects the aspirations of Global South countries for solidarity and cooperation, he said.
China supports Iran in safeguarding its sovereignty and security, and is willing to work with Iran to further advance bilateral relations, Wang added.
Bagheri Kani told Wang that Iran stands ready to promote the steady development of bilateral ties and strengthen cooperation with China in international and multilateral frameworks.

articles.title_orig: Defense, healthcare, crypto and AI: How the midterm election could affect stocks
articles.title_zh: Defense, healthcare, crypto and AI: How the midterm election could affect stocks
articles.content_orig:
Lockheed Martin gets about 70% of its sales from the U.S. government. Medicaid accounts for three-quarters of Molina Healthcare's premium revenue . Coinbase is waiting on Congress to finish writing the rules for cryptocurrency .
For some of the biggest U.S. companies, Washington is part of the business model. Now, the midterm election could change who holds the leverage.
A Democratic victory in either or both chambers of Congress would grant the party new leverage to investigate companies , challenge federal spending and demand legislative concessions. But their reach would have limits: President Donald Trump would retain his veto and broad authority over tariffs, immigration and federal regulation.
Historically, stocks have performed well under divided government. Under Republican presidents, the S&P 500 has gained an average of 23% in the year after midterms when Congress was split, compared with 16% when Democrats controlled both chambers, according to a Morgan Stanley analysis published Thursday. Analysts often attribute the pattern in part to congressional gridlock limiting sweeping policy changes.
Still, some analysts caution against assuming that pattern will repeat.
"We don't think that blueprint holds up this time around, and we still see plenty of reasons to be constructive on the U.S. equity market," said Ariana Salvatore , head of U.S. public policy research at Morgan Stanley.
For investors, the midterm election could reshape which businesses preserve their advantages in Washington, particularly in industries such as defense , healthcare , banking and artificial intelligence .
"There are some policy changes that might be market moving, at least for certain segments," said Jeff Buchbinder , chief equity strategist at LPL Financial.
Control of either the House or Senate would give Democrats committee gavels and subpoena power, allowing them to demand documents, compel testimony and haul executives before public hearings.
Companies are already getting a preview.
On Oct. 21, Sen. Richard Blumenthal , D-Conn., the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, sought records tied to Trump's White House ballroom from donors including Cisco , Salesforce , ServiceNow and Kraken . Apple and Nvidia each committed $25 million to the project, according to records obtained by The Washington Post .
Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., has separately sought records involving tariff exclusions, including communications involving Apple's former CEO Tim Cook , as Democrats investigate whether Trump used trade policy to reward political allies and donors.
While donations do not prove wrongdoing or favorable treatment, congressional probes still carry risks: subpoenas consume executive bandwidth, reveal internal communications and generate unpredictable news coverage. Few CEOs relish the idea of sitting at a witness table before lawmakers and television cameras.
"It creates volatility because you get a negative headline," said Monica Guerra , Morgan Stanley's head of policy and geopolitical strategy, who expects Democrats to cast a wide net for their probes.
Democrats have signaled interest in Trump family businesses, government contractors, firms tied to Donald Trump Jr.'s 1789 Capital and companies associated with Elon Musk and DOGE .
Then there is the most basic power Congress has: deciding where the money goes.
Trump's 2025 tax cuts and spending law, known as One Big Beautiful Bill , is projected to reduce federal Medicaid spending by $911 billion through 2034, according to a KFF analysis of Congressional Budget Office estimates. KFF is a nonpartisan nonprofit that provides health policy information. Meanwhile, new work requirements for Medicaid enrollees are scheduled to take effect Jan. 1, or earlier in some states, while tighter state budgets could mean fewer are people covered and greater pressure on provider payments.
Molina Healthcare generated $32.2 billion , or 75% of its 2025 premium revenue, from Medicaid, according to the company's annual SEC filing. In the same filing, Molina warned that losing government contracts or failing to renew them on favorable terms could materially reduce premium revenue.
A Democratic-controlled chamber could not repeal the 2025 law on its own but could use must-pass budget negotiations to seek funding changes or delays to some cuts.
"They're probably going to push back on those Medicaid cuts," Buchbinder told CNBC, noting that preserving coverage could help stabilize enrollment for Medicaid insurers and patient volumes for hospitals.
Hospitals face their own squeeze: fewer insured patients can mean more uncompensated care, while state budget pressure can reduce reimbursement rates, according to KFF. Congress created a $50 billion rural health fund over five years to cushion some of the blow, but KFF and medical providers have said the money would not fully offset the broader Medicaid reductions.
Democratic gains could still cut both ways for healthcare. The same lawmakers seeking to protect Medicaid funding could also intensify scrutiny of insurers, hospitals and drugmakers over prices, coverage and profits.
Defense contractors face a fight over which weapons and programs Congress keeps funding. The White House has requested $1.5 trillion for national defense in fiscal 2027, with a focus on replenishing weapons, bolstering readiness and covering other needs, some tied to the Iran war .
The White House has requested $1.5 trillion for national defense in fiscal 2027, while separately seeking an $87.6 billion supplemental appropriation from Congress for fiscal 2026, driven primarily by military operations related to Iran.
A Democratic Congress could challenge some Iran- and Israel-related spending while pushing for more aid to Ukraine . However, bipartisan consensus on China deterrence, nuclear modernization and missile defense could protect other major programs, according to multiple analysts.
For contractors, the difference could mean billions of dollars in orders.
Lockheed Martin, for example, recently reached a framework agreement with the Pentagon covering 850 F-35 fighter jets over a decade. But the agreement is not yet a finalized contract: Congress must authorize the multiyear purchase and provide the funding.
"You want to be a stock picker and not just ride the whole sector," Guerra told CNBC, pointing to areas such as shipbuilding, autonomous systems and missile defense as likely winners.
For crypto companies, the midterms could determine whether Trump's regulatory shift becomes durable law or remains vulnerable to the next administration. The industry's push for permanence stalled in September, when the Senate failed to advance the Trump-backed Clarity Act , a sweeping market-structure bill.
Shares of Coinbase and stablecoin issuer Circle fell as much as 11% when the measure failed.
Getting a bill through the next Congress could come at a price. Democratic gains would give the party more leverage to demand stricter consumer safeguards, limits on yield-bearing stablecoins and tighter scrutiny of Trump's crypto businesses.
"In some ways, the industry doesn't really care who got elected," said Sam Stovall , chief investment strategist at CFRA Research. "They just want to know what the rules are going to be for the coming year."
Banks are looking for durability, too.
Federal regulators estimate their proposed capital overhau l would cut requirements for the largest banks by roughly 4.8% , potentially freeing billions for lending and shareholder payouts. The Federal Reserve writes the rules, but Senate control shapes who fills future vacancies, and congressional committees can pressure regulators through hearings and investigations.
"It's at the regulatory level where stuff can happen that matters," Buchbinder said.
AI may be the messiest political trade of all.

articles.title_orig: Government making up China policy as it goes along, say MPs
articles.title_zh: Government making up China policy as it goes along, say MPs
articles.content_orig:
By SAM MERRIMAN, POLITICAL CORRESPONDENT
Published: 20:12 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 22:07 EDT, 1 November 2026
Ministers have been accused of jeopardising national security by prioritising 'diplomatic politeness' with China .
A report from MPs today criticises Labour's approach to Beijing as the 'worst of both worlds'.
In a devastating indictment of its dealings with the communist state, the chairman of the business, innovation, science and trade committee (Bist) said the 'Government keeps making up its China policy as it goes along'.
Firms have missed out on lucrative commercial deals as Britain has been left increasingly exposed to 'unquantified, unmanaged risk', the report adds.
Last night the committee put pressure on the Prime Minister to clarify his stance on closer dealings with the Chinese Communist Party.
'We await confirmation of how much continuity there is between the approaches to China of the Starmer and Burnham governments,' the MPs said.
Last year Labour, under Sir Keir Starmer, refused to publish a Government review of relations with China, releasing only a short summary and arguing that publishing the full findings could damage British interests.
In June, two men were convicted of running 'shadow policing' operations on British soil, spying on Chinese dissidents and MPs who supported them.
Labour ministers have been accused of jeopardising national security by prioritising 'diplomatic politeness' with China. Pictured: PM Andy Burnham, then Mayor of Manchester, with China's Consul General Tang Rui on April 17, 2026
Labour's Ed Miliband shakes hands with Wang Hongzhi, head of China's National Energy Administration, at the China-UK Energy Dialogue in Beijing, China on March 17, 2025
Labour was accused of pandering to China after plans for a new mega embassy on the old Royal Mint site were approved in January, despite spying fears. Pictured: A concept grapohic for the proposed embassy
Labour was accused of pandering to China after plans for a new mega embassy on the old Royal Mint site near the Tower of London were approved in January, despite spying fears.
Shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat has described the report as 'damning' and accused Labour of overseeing a dereliction of its duty to the public.
He told the Daily Mail: 'Labour are distracted and allowing Beijing to dictate terms, risking economic dependence on a hostile China. This is unacceptable. The Government's disjointed, last-minute approach leaves Britain weak and susceptible to Chinese control.'
The report warns that 'low-cost, increasingly sophisticated Chinese-connected technology has proliferated in the UK' and says the Government should create a register of high-risk firms to combat the threat associated with this.
It concludes: 'We are disappointed that, in failing to create a register of high-risk jurisdictions, the Government has prioritised diplomatic politeness over the UK's national security.' However, the Government last night rejected the Bist committee report and said it 'disagrees with its conclusion'.
The committee found that Labour has re-engaged with Beijing 'without establishing the rules of the game'.
Its chairman, Labour MP Liam Byrne, said: 'Businesses cannot plan for the future when the Government keeps making up its China policy as it goes along. Ministers promised clarity and consistency.
'Instead, we have opportunities missed, risks unmanaged and decisions left until the eleventh hour. Britain must shape its own relationship with China, or risk having that relationship shaped for us in Washington or Beijing.'
China's President Xi Jinping, right, and Britain's then Prime Minister Keir Starmer, left, shake hands before their meeting at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing on January 29, 2026
Bill Yuen, 65, (l) and Peter Wai, 41, (r) were convicted in June following a trial at the Old Bailey. Wai was found guilty of running a Chinese 'state intelligence service' on British soil while working as a UK Border Force officer, on the orders of former Hong Kong superintendent Yuen
The report also found products made with slave labour by repressed Uyghur Muslims ending up on British shelves. Pictured: Buildings north of Kashgar in China's northwestern Xinjiang region believed to be a re-education camp where mostly Muslim ethnic minorities are detained
Should Britain risk national security for economic ties and diplomatic relations with China?
Mr Byrne added that 'we should welcome trade that builds Britain's strength' but cease dealings that 'put that strength at risk'.
The committee recognised that disengaging from China is neither realistic nor desirable as annual trade with Beijing is now £140billion a year – about 7 per cent of total UK trade.
However it added that changes need to be made as the Government's decision-making on China – such as the takeover of British Steel from the firm's Chinese owners at a cost of £1.3million a day – has been characterised by 'reactivity, inconsistency, and opacity'.
MPs also raised concerns about the increasing adoption of cheap Chinese electric cars. These devices pose a risk to national security through spying and the ability to control vehicles remotely is a 'potential risk to life', the report adds.
The report is also damning on the risk of products made with slave labour by repressed Uyghur Muslims in the Xinjiang region ending up on British shelves.
In order to reset Britain's relationship with China, MPs have called on the Government to 'insist on fair trade' to create a 'level playing field'. Ministers should also 'prevent the transfer of sensitive technologies and data to China'.
A Government spokesman said: 'Our approach to China is consistent – we will co-operate where we can and challenge where we must.
'Our Trade Strategy makes clear that we will capitalise on every opportunity to grow our economy while never compromising on national security. Increased discussions with China allow us to directly raise concerns where they arise.'
DAILY MAIL COMMENT: It's time to drop the 'diplomatic politeness' and change your tune on China, PM...

articles.title_orig: Iranians have left Doha talks, draft proposal for US deal being circulated, official says
articles.title_zh: Iranians have left Doha talks, draft proposal for US deal being circulated, official says
articles.content_orig:
Iranian negotiators were in Doha on Sunday for a third consecutive day of talks with Qatari mediators aimed at pushing for a deal to end the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, an official briefed on the discussions told Reuters.
The talks come amid concerns that the conflict could escalate again after the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections . U.S. President Donald Trump has said the United States will not launch new attacks on Iran before the vote and that talks with Tehran have been productive, though he has not ruled out further military action afterward.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday that the purpose of the "ongoing and progressing" talks was to continue consultations with the Qatari mediators, adding Tehran is prepared for "both defense and diplomacy."
Speaking to state media, Araqchi said discussions on a "two-day proposal" were continuing, but that no final conclusion had been reached.
Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera quoted Araqchi as saying in an interview on Saturday that Iranian and Qatari negotiators had developed a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days of a potential agreement with Washington.
Iran has repeatedly said it would respond to any new attacks by striking US and Israeli targets in neighboring countries, as the eight-month-old war continues to disrupt global oil supplies and spill over across the Middle East.
"We are doing our best in this process, and we hope that there is rationality on the other side so that they prioritize diplomacy over other paths," Araqchi said of the talks with Qatari officials.
Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei on Saturday ordered the armed forces to be prepared for any attack, while the military later announced steps to strengthen its readiness.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that Trump has not decided whether to launch new strikes against Iran, but would prefer to resolve the conflict diplomatically.
Qatari mediators were in Tehran on Friday for discussions with Iranian officials before moving the talks to Doha on Saturday, an official had told Reuters. The talks were being coordinated in regular contacts with Washington, the official added.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Negotiation push for U.S.-Iran deal punctuated by threats to resume fighting
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Negotiation push for U.S.-Iran deal punctuated by threats to resume fighting
articles.content_orig:
Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson said Monday that the next move in the standoff with the United States is for President Trump to make.
"The ball is in the U.S. court, because our demands have been stated very clearly and transparently, and Iran's demands are reasonable and logical," Esmaeil Baqaei told journalists in Tehran.
Baqaei said ongoing negotiations, which have been brokered by Qatar, Pakistan and other mediators, were centered around the a seven-day proposal that Iran originally presented to the U.S. side in September, which calls for frozen Iranian assets to be released, the U.S. naval blockade to be lifted and an end to fighting on all fronts, in exchange for the phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and further negotiations on other topics.
President Trump rejected the initial proposal, but both sides have since exchanged revisions, and Mr. Trump has said repeatedly in recent weeks that he just needs to make a decision on whether to launch new attacks on Iran, or to make a deal to end the war.
Speaking Sunday to a radio network ahead of a campaign rally in Iowa, Mr. Trump said he would finish with the war soon, "one way or the other."
"Either they'll make a deal, or we'll just end it," he said, without offering any further context.
President Trump told reporters Sunday that he'd spoken with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday and had a "very good talk with him."
Mr. Trump gave no details but said the two had discussed the war in Iran.
According to sources cited by Axios , Netanyahu pushed for Mr. Trump to strike Iran but the president wants to let the negotiations play out.
The U.S. and Iran both engaged in indirect talks via mediators led by Qatar who are pushing to strike a deal between both sides before the conflict escalated.
Mr. Trump has repeatedly hinted he is considering resuming attacks on Iran after the midterm elections.
Qatari mediators are leading indirect talks aimed at reaching a deal between the U.S. and Iran, but the closed door negotiations have been punctuated by exchanges of threats between the leaders of both countries.
Iranian negotiators are in Qatar for talks on a proposal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz soon, according to Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who added the outcome depends on answers provided by the United States.
On Saturday, President Trump said the U.S. still had to "take care of" one or two more potential targets in Iran, citing a suspected nuclear complex at Pickaxe Mountain. On Sunday he reiterated the threat, saying he may have to give Tehran "the hammer" at some unspecified time.
Meanwhile, Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei warned on Saturday there would be no "geographical limitations" should the fighting with the U.S. resume, adding that there is a "vast theatre" to inflict damage.
Both sides have previously acknowledged that indirect talks are underway but consistently exchange threats.
The United Arab Emirates' presidential adviser said Sunday that his country hopes a diplomatic breakthrough in Qatar-led mediations is possible, but that they are also preparing for the possibility of escalation.
Speaking at a security forum in Bahrain, Anwar Gargash said Iran's attacks on Gulf countries such as the UAE made this a "watershed year" for the region.
"We don't really want to see another round of confrontation in the region," Gargash told the audience. But he added that his country and the region are braced for the "the worst," referring to the resumption of active hostilities.
The UAE was consistently targeted by Tehran in the opening weeks of the war in retribution for U.S. strikes on Iran, disrupting tourism and daily life, and effectively throwing the security landscape of the region into question.
A vessel was struck on Sunday by "an unknown projectile" in the Strait of Hormuz, a British maritime security agency said, after Qatari media reported an earlier attack on a gas tanker.
Britain's UKMTO maritime agency said "the master of a merchant vessel has relayed a mayday call... stating that another vessel has been struck by an unknown projectile" in the strait.
Earlier, Qatar's state news agency said a Qatari gas tanker had been attacked on Friday with "unidentified objects" while transiting Gulf waters. None of the crew members onboard the vessel were injured, and there was no environmental impact from the attack, the report said.
The attack struck a liquefied natural gas carrier, Al Mayeda, which belongs to the Qatar Gas Transport Company, Qatar News Agency said.
Since the Middle East war began in February, Iran has been targeting vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Gulf in an effort to assert control over shipping.
President Trump said he believes the U.S. will soon put the war with Iran away, "one way or the other."
The president was speaking to Right Side Broadcasting Network before a campaign rally in Iowa on Sunday.
"We've had such a victory, and we'll put it away very soon, one way or the other," Mr. Trump said. "Either they'll make a deal, or we'll just end it… The job we've done is amazing."
Earlier Sunday, Iran's top diplomat said he hopes there is "rationality" on the U.S. side as diplomatic efforts seek to avert a return to all-out war.

articles.title_zh: Initial results show Bulgaria's acting president Yotova wins runoff election
articles.content_orig:
Acting President Iliana Yotova is the apparent winner of Bulgaria ’s presidential runoff, initial results of the vote count on Sunday showed.
The race for the largely ceremonial post had pitted Yotova, an ally of Prime Minister Rumen Radev, against Andrey Gyurov, a banker and former caretaker prime minister backed by the pro-Western opposition.
Yotova gained between 57.4% and 58.2% of the vote, according to estimates from several polling institutes, well ahead of Gyurov, who garnered between 38.6% and 39.6%.
If confirmed by official results, Yotova would become Bulgaria’s first elected female head of state.
Gyurov conceded defeat saying that “this is how the Bulgarian citizens have voted,” and added that the results had to be accepted as they stood.
The war in Ukraine, close to Bulgaria’s borders, played a significant role in the election in this country on NATO’s eastern flank.
Throughout the campaign, Yotova repeatedly advocated a peaceful solution for Ukraine through negotiations with Russia. She said she wanted to be a “President of Peace” for Bulgaria.
Gyurov, in contrast, signalled closer alignment with Western partners and stronger support for Ukraine in the face of Russia’s war of aggression.
The vote was the first major test for the Moscow-friendly Progressive Bulgaria party of Prime Minister Rumen Radev, which endorsed Yotova. The 62-year-old took over the presidency in January, when Radev stepped down to run for parliament.
Observers expect her to continue Radev’s policy of keeping Bulgaria on its European path, while also supporting better relations with Russia and the lifting of sanctions.
The election in this south-eastern EU country was overshadowed by the conflict in Ukraine. In recent weeks, drone attacks on merchant ships have become increasingly frequent in Bulgaria’s economic zone in the Black Sea, as well as in that of neighbouring Romania.
Bulgaria’s presidency is primarily ceremonial. The head of state has no executive powers, and all major policies must be approved by parliament. However, direct election gives the president greater political authority. The president leads the armed forces, can veto legislation, signs international treaties and appoints ambassadors.
Presidents in Bulgaria are directly elected for a five-year term and can serve no more than two terms.

articles.title_orig: King Charles Meets Both Joy and Criticism on Caribbean Tour
articles.title_zh: King Charles Meets Both Joy and Criticism on Caribbean Tour
articles.content_orig:
It has been three years since Willem-Alexander said sorry, so please use your trip to the Caribbean to follow his example
You are currently on a Caribbean royal tour through the Bahamas, Guyana, and Antigua and Barbuda. I understand that during this tour you will not issue a formal apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade, or address the role your own family played in it. You will instead express your “sorrow”, and this will make it easier for politicians to also dodge the question. Whether that is Kemi Badenoch calling an apology a “navel-gazing distraction ”, or the prime minister, Andy Burnham, saying he would support an apology, while flatly opposing reparations.
Coincidentally, I’m also in the middle of a world tour for the English translation of my book, Jaguarman, a novel about how my enslaved Surinamese ancestors survived 300 years of hell on Earth. I travelled from Ghana to Indonesia to New York, when I was asked to respond to you, as soon as possible. That’s how it often goes in this strange story, I’ve noticed: people like you get centuries to find the right words, while we must scramble to respond to your actions. But, yes, I do have something to say.
Three years ago your Dutch counterpart, King Willem-Alexander, stood before an audience of people of colour, many of them my friends. Dressed up like kings and queens, they listened solemnly as he did what you will not and apologised for the role of the Dutch state in enslaving our ancestors , and for the failure of his own family, the house of Orange-Nassau, to act against it. Slavery was “a crime against humanity”, he said, “and the stadholders and kings of the house of Orange-Nassau did nothing to stop it”.
It was a moment that people on whose shoulders I stand had fought for for centuries, often at the risk of their health or even their lives. Willem-Alexander’s speech was directed at people of colour such as me. But I felt that the apology was perhaps even more important for the rest of the population.
It happened in 2023, on 1 July, the day the Netherlands commemorates the abolition of slavery, a celebration called Keti Koti. In the Netherlands, many institutions tend only to invite writers such as me to speak on this one particular day, so as Willem-Alexander was addressing the nation, I was somewhere else, in a small library, in front of an audience of mostly white people, giving my own lecture about what they could learn from my Black ancestors.
We from the colonial diaspora already know the true history of our mother country. We already know what the powers that govern us are capable of. We know the darkness they can create. And we also know that it is possible to come through that darkness. To me, the apology was most important for all these other people who thought my history had nothing to do with them. For those who had never considered that there might be something to learn from the people who gave me this life.
after newsletter promotion
You know the truth, Willem-Alexander knows it, I know it, but many of your subjects do not. The truth is my ancestors were kidnapped. Chained. Trafficked across the ocean. Sold. Torn from one another. Turned into property. Brainwashed. Silenced. Mocked. Cursed. But the fire inside us was never extinguished. Despite the plantations. Despite the Atlantic. Despite the slave forts. That is why I am alive.
That is not a small thing. It is enormous. That’s why the people receiving Willem-Alexander’s apology were dressed up like kings and queens. They know what a huge gift it is to be alive, and how important it is to take care of what you have been given. They know that they have not been put on this earth in order to wither. They have been put on this earth to blossom. And even if all your freedom is taken away from you by other people, you can find ways to flourish, because the spark of life itself is on our side.
Its fire will keep burning, your majesty, whether you apologise or not. The true heroes in this history were rarely born as royalty. But, of course, being born as royalty doesn’t prevent you from doing the right thing. You cannot stop the truth from coming out. But you can choose whether history remembers you as someone who stood in its way, or someone who stood with it.
Raoul de Jong is a Dutch novelist

“I think I’m going to switch back to my other iPhone.”
I’ll admit, I said this multiple times during my five-day vacation with the new iPhone Duo, after encountering frustrations with broken apps, unfamiliar gestures (a return to Touch ID, argh !), and camera concerns that had me lugging around two phones.
By the time the trip was over, I didn’t want to go back.
When I first unboxed the Duo, a loaner from Apple, I was genuinely intrigued. I felt a flutter of anticipation as I peeled back the factory seal wrap and booted up the device. In retrospect, this was probably the first signal that Duo was going to ultimately win me over.
As a tech reporter, I’ve received a lot of test devices over the years, so unfortunately, opening a package with a new gadget inside is no longer the thrill it used to be. But sometime in the days leading up to the Duo’s ship date, I found myself actually wanting one – I had started doing the math and comparing upgrade options that would allow me to afford the $2K the phone would cost. I started scrolling TikTok reviews of Duo cases . I hesitated not only because of the price but because moving to the Duo is a major change – especially coming from an iPhone 17 Pro Max. The phones could not be more different.
As I was about to head out on vacation when the Duo arrived, I decided to tote my 17 Pro Max with me too, as something of a safety net. I ended up using the Duo more, and grew comfortable with it over the course of the trip, despite some frustrations.
There’s always a psychological switching cost in changing phones, but particularly going from a high-end phone to a more experimental device like the Duo. For someone used to the iPhone’s long-perfected tech and thin rectangular shape, the Duo’s short, squat, and decidedly novel nature was somewhat off-putting at first.
“Where is all that screen real estate I used to have?” I lamented. “Will this thing even fit comfortably in my pocket?”
As it turns out, it does. Front and back pockets, in fact. Even while wearing a case. You can sit down with it in your back pocket, effectively squashing it, and it does not break. (I meant to be more careful, but I forgot to be, repeatedly, as I tend to carry phones in my back pocket when walking around. I sat on the phone countless times. It’s clearly not that fragile.)
I also dropped the phone (by accident!) at least three times. Twice from about table height and once when it got pushed off the side of the bed. It did not fall on soft carpet, but rather on concrete, tile, and wood floors. It didn’t break then either, and the screen didn’t crack. I wouldn’t call these professional drop tests by any means, but it certainly was a relief for someone fairly clumsy with their phone.
Of course, I did encounter some frustrations. I had to scroll more to read back through text threads because of the Duo’s small outer screen; unoptimized apps with numerous controls sometimes had key features tucked away in a “more” (three-dot) menu, leading to a hunt to find the option you needed; and, on multiple occasions, the Google Search app just froze.
Though not Apple’s fault, the latter turned out to be my biggest annoyance software-wise, given that Search is one of my go-to apps especially when traveling. On vacation, I open the app repeatedly to look up points of interest, restaurant reviews, distances between towns, weather, and more. But Google’s app would just stop working, and tapping its back button did nothing.
This seemed to be a problem specific to the Search app’s AI Mode, which these days you’re often dropped into without actually requesting it. (Even more reason to be annoyed by AI Search!) The workaround has been to force-close the app, so the next time you open it, your returned to the home screen with the search box. (It amazes me that, in a time when Google is facing a search decline because of AI, it wouldn’t have prioritized making its Search app functional on Apple’s latest device!)
In addition, many of the early reviews pointed out how many apps were not updated or redesigned for Duo at launch, which meant they had a telltale black bar on the side, cramping the limited screen real estate when the phone is closed even further. This is true, but personally speaking, I didn’t think it was a dealbreaker for making a switch to the Duo.
For one thing, companies have been pushing out their Duo-optimized updates fairly quickly. Those that have not – and there are still more than a few! – continue to be usable. They’re just kind of … ugly.
Google Maps was not Duo-optimized during the trip, yet I had no problem using it for driving directions, local search and discovery, route planning, and the like. If anything, the black-barred apps felt more like an aesthetic issue than a functional problem, even though they’re smaller than usual when the Duo is folded.
I expect all the major apps will eventually update. As for the older apps that never do? Well, it’s probably time to move on from apps no longer being maintained, I’d say, particularly in an era when older software is being exploited left and right by AI-enabled hacking tools.
However, I will agree with the other reviewers who complained about the lack of Face ID.
This is the Duo’s biggest drawback – not the screen, not the camera, not the lack of an Action button for launching your preferred AI assistant. It’s Touch ID.
It is much easier to look at your phone than to fiddle around with finger presses. While I easily avoided the need to use Touch ID to unlock the device – I am almost always wearing an Apple Watch, which serves as an alternative authentication method – I often stumbled when it came to using apps and Apple Pay.
Tap-and-pay is one of the areas where it’s immediately obvious how much smoother Face ID has made everyday tasks. Returning to Touch ID at the time of payment was cumbersome, given that you’re often holding shopping bags, a purse, and, in my case, a dog leash, in addition to the phone you’re using to pay with.
There’s a certain amount of what I guess I’ll call “muscle memory” that you have to overcome when you switch back to Touch ID. I found the easiest grip was to cradle the phone in your hand and use your thumb to authenticate. But where I repeatedly messed up was remembering to keep my thumb or finger on the Touch ID sensor long enough to authenticate. At times, my finger wasn’t situated quite right (I blame the dog pulling on the leash!), and I had to readjust. “I miss Face ID!,” I complained multiple times at checkout.
Though returning to Touch ID was something I got used to, it’s far from ideal. I can see this as being a real stopping point for some early adopters who would otherwise want to move to the Duo. It’s not an insurmountable problem, but it’s among the top reasons not to get the Duo now, in my opinion. (A future version is said to support Face ID .)
Another reason to be wary of the Duo? The camera. Much has been said about the Duo’s lesser camera system. The Duo has two rear cameras to my iPhone 17 Pro Max’s three. It has no telephoto lens. It has a 10x digital zoom versus the Pro’s 40x. The Pro has more advanced hardware for low-light photography and supports ProRAW, ProRes, and other advanced features.
Very simply put: if you are an iPhone photographer or a content creator, you shouldn’t consider the Duo as your primary device.
For, you know, us normal folks, the Duo’s camera is okay. Not great, but fine. What were you going to do with those photos you’re snapping anyway? Post them to Instagram Stories or Facebook? Text them to a friend? Look back on them fondly when they reappear in your photo widget on your Home Screen? Turn them into a Lock Screen wallpaper? None of these things requires a Pro-level camera.

Stock futures moved higher Monday as oil prices fell sharply and tech names rebounded, while investors braced for a packed week of earnings results, jobs reports and the upcoming midterm elections.
S&P 500 futures traded 0.5%, while Nasdaq-100 futures gained 0.8%. Futures linked to the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 310 points, or 0.6%.
Brent crude tumbled 4.5% to $108.38 per barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures also pulled back more than 4% to $99.31.
Micron, Sandisk and Western Digital rose more than 2% each. Nvidia and Microsoft also ticked higher in early trading.
The moves come after the major U.S. stock benchmarks suffered a losing week, bogged down by selling pressure in tech as investors continued to scrutinize names related to the artificial intelligence buildout.
Still, 3Fourteen Research's Warren Pies isn't too concerned. "I just don't see anything broken with the AI trade fundamentally," he said on CNBC's "Closing Bell Overtime" on Friday. "Technicals are another story."
The tech-heavy Nasdaq and the S&P 500 logged a losing October amid AI spending concerns, with the Nasdaq suffering its worst losses since March 2025. The Dow, however, rose almost 2% as investors rotated into defensive areas like healthcare.
"Rather than running for the hills amid heightened AI risks, investors are seeing plenty of return potential in other types of stocks," Mike Dickson, head of research and quantitative strategies at Horizon, said in a note last week.
Dickson added that while this week's midterm elections "have some investors worried that changes in Washington, D.C., could impact the markets, it's important to remember that stocks tend to stay steady regardless of which party gains control of Congress."
The elections will be held on Tuesday, when Democrats are expected to take control of the House of Representatives, while Senate control remains uncertain.
Investors are also awaiting October's nonfarm payrolls reading, which is scheduled for release on Friday and is expected to show an increase of 55,000 jobs on the month, according to economists polled by Dow Jones.
In addition to the closely watched monthly jobs report, a fresh round of earnings releases is also due this week. "Magnificent Seven" member Apple is scheduled to report after the bell on Monday. McDonald's and Qualcomm are slated to report later in the week.
In Europe, the Stoxx 600 benchmark was last 0.1% higher, reversing earlier losses. France's CAC 40 advanced 0.4%, followed by Germany's DAX , up 0.3%.
U.S. Treasury yields were mixed early Monday as investors gear up for another busy week of economic data and corporate earnings, as well as the midterm elections.
U.K. manufacturing production expanded at its fastest rate in more than two years in October, according to S&P Global Purchasing Managers' Index figures released on Monday.
Output and new orders grew at faster rates, confidence about the year ahead hit an eight-month high, and demand increased at home and abroad, though cost pressures and supply disruption remained elevated.
Rob Dobson, director at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said the sector showed "resilience" in the run-up to last week's budget , though a six-month run of increased hirings halted.
"The remainder of 2026 will see if the confirmed rise in the minimum wage for next year will continue to weigh on employment trends," Dobson said, adding that strong activity and high business costs would "further shorten the odds of interest rate hikes to come from the Bank of England."
Major U.S. AI stocks showed signs of recovery in premarket trading on Monday after shares of tech firms sold off last week amid concerns about an AI bubble.
SpaceX rose 3.2%, while AMD climbed 2.2%. Nvidia was up 1.5% and Micron 2.7%.
Neoclouds CoreWeave and Nebius were up 2.4% and 3%, respectively.
Eurozone manufacturing continued to grow in October. The S&P Global manufacturing purchasing managers' index came in at 52.7, down slightly from September's four-year high of 52.9 but above economists' forecast of 52.4. A reading above 50 signals growth.
Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said the figures point to the strongest run of manufacturing growth in the eurozone in more than four years.
He said rising defense spending, companies building up supplies and shifts in trade patterns linked to U.S. policies are helping support growth opportunities. These gains are partly offset by tariffs, conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, and the resulting pressure on supply chains and costs.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 was down 0.24% shortly after the market open, with the continent's major bourses moving lower and regional sectors mixed.
Travel and leisure stocks moved higher, gaining 0.72%, while European banks added 0.34%, and basic resources advanced 0.28%.
On the flipside, oil and gas names led losses, slipping 1.25%, as healthcare stocks shed 1.21%.
Among the continent's major bourses, only Italy's FTSE MIB showed a positive move in early dealmaking, rising 0.15% in Milan. The U.K.'s FTSE 100 dipped 0.34% in London, as the French CAC 40 shed 0.21% in Paris. Germany's DAX was down 0.03% in Frankfurt.
Asian markets were closed mixed on Monday, with Australia and Japan markets down, but other markets are in positive territory.
Australia S&P/ASX 200 was 0.58% down at 8,856.5, while Japan's Nikkei 225 gained 0.33% to 63,081.86.
South Korea's Kospi led gains with a 2.38% rise to 5,859.08, while the small-cap Kosdaq added 1.38% to close at 734.36.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index gained 0.44% in its last hour of trade, while mainland China's CSI 300 added 0.79%.
Oil prices retreated sharply early Monday amid reports that the U.S. and Iran are seeking diplomatic options to end the eight-month-long conflict in the Middle East.
Brent crude futures , the international price benchmark, were down 3.02% at $110.01 per barrel at 1:20 a.m. E.T.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for December delivery dropped 3.31% to $100.65.
Stock markets in Europe are expected to begin the first trading day of November in positive territory.
Stoxx 50 futures were seen moving 0.38% higher ahead of the market open.
France's CAC 40 is set to start the session up 0.33%, with the Italian FTSE MIB advancing 0.21%, and Germany's DAX rising 0.18%.
The U.K's FTSE 100 , in contrast, is expected to trade 0.12% lower when markets open.
Mainland China and Hong Kong shares open higher after reports that Chinese financial regulators will meet banks and securities firms to discuss measures aimed at bolstering the country’s stock market.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index gained 0.59%, while mainland China's CSI 300 added 0.21%.
The gains in Hang Seng were led by consumer cyclicals and tech sectors, up 0.48% each.
Shares of Kioxia fell around 14%, after the company cautioned that prices for flash memory are stalling, during its earnings call last Friday.
According to the Japanese semiconductor memory solutions firm, the average selling prices of NAND flash memory grew in the mid-20% range for the three months to September, compared with 70% in the prior quarter.
Kioxia also expects to deliver a 2 trillion yen in operating profit for the current quarter, but that was lower than what analysts had expected at 2.35 trillion yen. This suggests that prices increases were nearly flat on-quarter.
Asia-Pacific markets traded lower early Monday, tracking Wall Street's overall losses last week that was weighed by selling pressure in the tech sector.

articles.title_zh: Robots strut their stuff, race up sacred China mountain, some carrying eggs and watermelons
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of robots took on more than 3,000 steps up one of China's most famous peaks Monday, many carrying eggs and watermelons in a race organizers billed as a test of real-world machine endurance, state media showed.
For hundreds of years, Mount Tai -- the tallest peak in China's eastern Shandong province -- was an important pilgrimage for Chinese emperors, and it features prominently in Chinese mythology.
But the rugged terrain would prove a stern test for some competitors. One humanoid robot wearing a bandana collapsed in a heap on the cobbled route before engineers rushed in to repair it, while another tumbled down a flight of stairs and came to rest beside a rubbish bin.
The UNESCO World Heritage site hosted technologies of the future as part of a new World Mountain Robot Challenge, footage from state broadcaster CCTV showed.
Over a 2.4-mile course with more than 1,970 feet of ascent, robots and their engineers from around 90 teams were tasked with either completing the route as fast as possible or transporting fragile goods such as fresh eggs and watermelons to the summit.
A canine robot made by Beijing Lingyi Technology -- a subsidiary of industry giant Unitree -- completed the course in 43 minutes, 41 seconds, to win the four-legged speed category.
Most tourists take at least two hours to complete the route, according to CCTV.
The fastest humanoid robot -- belonging to Beijing-based team Zhishen Lingyue -- completed a shorter race course in 27 minutes and 26 seconds.
Organizers called Mount Tai's rocky terrain a "natural extreme testing ground" that could help train robots for real-world use, local media reported.
The race, organized by the state-run China Media Group, featured cash prizes for winners in several categories, including the fastest robots and the best load-carrying four-legged machine.

articles.title_zh: Global shares are mixed and US futures advance, while oil prices fall nearly 4%
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
By Stefano Rebaudo and Wayne Cole
Nov 2 (Reuters) - European stocks struggled for direction on Monday after Friday's tech rout, with investors looking ahead to Apple's earnings and taking comfort from a sharp fall in oil prices amid hopes for ‌a deal to end the Iran war.
Markets face a pivotal week, with investors still digesting the Federal Reserve's and the European ‌Central Bank's latest policy decisions, earnings season in full swing and the US midterm elections on Tuesday.
Euro zone government bond yields were little changed after last week's rally, but ​investor sentiment remained fragile amid concerns over France's fiscal outlook and continuing street unrest.
MSCI's main world stocks index <.MIWD00000PUS> was roughly unchanged, while Europe's STOXX 600 .STOXX was up 0.05%, with tech stocks rising 0.40%.
Nasdaq futures climbed 0.76% and S&P 500 futures increased 0.34%. The S&P 500 index <.SPX> fell 1.82% on Friday, while the Nasdaq tumbled 2.86%.
Japan's Nikkei .N225 dropped 0.33%, while South Korea's added 2.24%, having shed 16% last month.
Investors remain cautious ahead of the US ‌vote, with European stock markets facing a different ⁠set of challenges from their US counterparts.
"Further expected downside for the Euro area PMI is a drag on our Stoxx 600 forecast trajectory," wrote Sebastian Raedler, head of European equity strategy at BofA.
"However, the main reason for our caution ⁠on European equities is the risk of disappointment in the AI capex cycle as AI models commoditise and competitive moats prove limited."
Investors expect US equities to come under pressure in the event of a Democratic sweep, as markets price in the risk of higher corporate taxes and tighter AI regulation.
Opinion polls ​suggest ​Democrats are favoured to win the House, while the Senate remains too close ​to call, leaving the party well short of a veto-proof ‌two-thirds majority.
Apple has been an oasis of relative calm given it does not spend billions on data centres, and its shares have climbed for four straight months, helping it overtake Nvidia as the world's most valuable listed company.
Goldman Sachs analysts expect capital spending by hyperscalers to nearly double to $800 billion this year and rise further to $1.2 trillion in 2027. At the same time, they see S&P 500 earnings per share growth slowing to 18% next year from nearly 30% in 2026.
"Earnings results have underscored the fundamental challenge facing equity investors," wrote Ben Snider, Goldman's chief ‌US equity strategist, in a note.
US DOLLAR SAFE-HAVEN STATUS UNDER SCRUTINY
In foreign exchange ​markets, major currencies were largely subdued. The euro rose 0.37% to $1.1199, while the dollar ​was barely changed at 157.72 yen.
Rising oil prices tend to hurt ​the euro and yen as they worsen the outlook for energy-importing economies.
Investors are also questioning the dollar's safe-haven ‌status, concerned that a renewed tech-driven market selloff could ​weaken the US currency.
George Saravelos, global head ​of forex strategy at Deutsche Bank, said the US's reliance on foreign equity inflows was historically unprecedented and evidence showed that when the source of an equity shock is US-centric the dollar-equity correlation flips to positive.
Among central banks meeting this week, markets ​are pricing in rate increases from the Reserve Bank ‌of Australia, Bank of England and Riksbank, while the Norges Bank is seen on hold.
Data due this week include the ​US ISM manufacturing survey for October later on Monday and the closely watched non-farm payrolls report on Friday.
(Reporting by ​Stefano Rebaudo and Wayne Cole. Editing by Muralikumar Anantharaman and Mark Potter)

articles.title_orig: Iranian Tankers Bypass U.S. Naval Blockade to Transport Gas to China
articles.title_zh: Iranian Tankers Bypass U.S. Naval Blockade to Transport Gas to China
articles.content_orig:
A report by Fox News, citing the advocacy group “United Against Nuclear Iran” (UANI), reveals that at least nine tankers carrying Iranian oil or liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) have successfully bypassed U.S. maritime restrictions since the reimposition of the American naval blockade in July 2026.
According to the report, published on the evening of Sunday, November 1, 2026, tankers belonging to the Islamic Republic’s so-called “ghost fleet” are utilising maritime routes around Malaysia to transport sanctioned Iranian energy cargoes to China.
Following months of investigation, UANI published images of a tanker named “SOGL,” which departed from the port of Asaluyeh in late August 2026, carrying approximately 500,000 barrels of liquefied petroleum gas. After breaking through the U.S. naval blockade, the vessel reached Malaysian waters.
Jemima Shelley, a senior analyst at UANI, told Fox News that the tanker refuelled in waters near Malaysia and, after receiving support services, delivered its cargo to the port of Qinzhou in China.
According to Shelley, some smaller Iranian tankers turn off their tracking systems, sail under false flags, or conduct ship-to-ship transfers at sea to evade detection.
The UANI analyst noted that while the U.S. blockade has severely curtailed Iran’s crude oil exports, certain smaller tankers still manage to slip through.
Fox News further reported that China now serves as the destination for almost “all of Iran’s oil and LPG exports,” with Malaysian maritime corridors playing a critical role in sustaining this trade.

articles.content_orig:
Apollo Global Management has launched a European private credit platform with more than 10 billion euros ($11.2 billion) of lending capacity, backed by several blue-chip investors, including the Abu Dhabi Investment Council (ADIC).
The European Credit Company will invest in performing credit across the large and mid-market sectors, including corporate and asset-backed lending, as well as lending to real-asset owners in infrastructure and real estate.
The venture is led by Giacomo Petrobelli, serving as chief executive officer, and Christian Meissner, its chairman.
Petrobelli said Apollo's ECC aims to capitalize on a "generational opportunity" to finance Europe's long-term growth agenda using global pools of capital.
The venture's backing from ADIC comes a week after Apollo agreed to buy a nearly 10% stake in Mubadala Capital, the alternative asset manager subsidiary of Mubadala Investment Co., Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund.
Other strategic partners in the new platform include European insurance group Athora, Japanese lender Norinchukin Bank, Standard Chartered and Aranda Principal Strategies, a U.S. credit investor, Apollo said in an announcement.
"We aim to build ECC into a premier pan-European credit platform, focused exclusively on the region, with deep local relationships, differentiated sourcing and flexible solutions that span all credit types," said Petrobelli.
"The Global Industrial Renaissance is creating tremendous financing needs around the world that are acutely felt in Europe, whether it's energy transition and transmission, defense, or digital and traditional infrastructure," added Apollo president Jim Zelter.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine and Russia air raid apps hacked to send fake radiation alerts
articles.title_zh: Ukraine and Russia air raid apps hacked to send fake radiation alerts
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine and Russia both claimed their emergency alert apps were hacked on Sunday night, and made to send false alerts to residents warning of air raids and other attacks, including nuclear.
Shortly before 23:00 local time (21:00 GMT), Ukraine's widely used air raid app sent red-level air raid warnings nation-wide, with additional warnings of radiation, chemical attacks, and street fighting sent to some residents in areas including Kyiv.
An alert on Telegram read: "The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel."
A few hours later Russian authorities said its app was hacked. A Ukrainian espionage group claimed fake warnings of nuclear strikes inside Russia had been sent to users.
In Ukraine, the Central Intelligence Agency said there had been a failure in the app, and urged people to use other sources of information to clarify the situation on the threat of air strikes.
The alerts started at approximately 22:47, with the first additional warning issued in Kyiv reading: "Radiation threat. Radiation threat declared in Kyiv."
The next message, written in Russian, came at 22:48, which read: "Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across Ukraine. Don't worry, it's Oreshnik flying". Oreshnik is the name of a Russian intermediate-range ballistic missile capable of carrying nuclear or conventional warheads.
Russia has the world's biggest nuclear arsenal, and President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly suggested an openness to using all weapons at Russia's disposal .
A third alert, at 22:49, again in Ukrainian, said: "Chemical threat. There is a threat of a chemical attack on Kyiv. Don't go outside."
At 22:49, a fourth alert stated there was a "Street fighting threat. Street fighting is taking place in Kyiv. Don't go outside."
At 23:53 a series of all clear messages were then delivered to users' phones, which were connected to each of the previous Kyiv alerts, individually declaring each threat clear.
The Central Intelligence Agency said on Telegram that the alerts triggered a radiation hazard signal on loudspeaker devices in the Lviv region but added there was no threat of radiation hazard.
The Air Alert app is supported by the Ministry of Digital Transformation of Ukraine, and informs users instantly about the beginning and end of defence alerts. The ministry said it temporarily disabled the app for maintenance after it had "apparently been compromised".
While the false alerts were quickly contained, cybersecurity experts suggested it was a new line in apparent Russian cyberattacks.
"I think it's the first time it's happened to an official Ukrainian information app, but I suspect it won't be the last," Herbert Lin, a senior research scholar for cyber policy and security at Stanford University, told BBC World Service's Newsday programme.
Oleksander Merezhko, chair of the foreign affairs committee in the Ukrainian parliament and a member of President Zelensky's Servant of the People party, told the BBC the attack didn't cause panic or extreme reaction. Merezhko said Ukrainians, especially in Kyiv, were used to "practically non-stop alerts".
"Secondly, this message was in Russian language which immediately aroused suspicions," he said.
"It's a very unpleasant fact but it is part of cyber war and people in Ukraine understand that. It is possible and we are quite prepared for such  possibilities."
If the alert app is not working, Ukraine's Centre for Countering Disinformation advises the public to turn on notifications on their smartphones, pay attention to sirens, and to only read official sources.
Several leaders of other regions also posted on Telegram that the app had apparently been hacked and there was no local threat.
"Everything is calm in the region for now," said Svitlana Onyshchuk, the head of the Ivano-Frankivsk region. The app had reported a red-level air raid alert for the region in Ukraine's east, between 22:50 and 23:57.
The Vinnytsia regional head, Natalya Zabolotna, said there had been a cyber-attack on the Air Alert app and posted a warning on Telegram not to click on the link in the message, which could be a phishing attempt.
A few hours after the false alerts in Ukraine, Russia's ministry of emergency situations said its app had been subjected to "a massive cyberattack", which sent "fake information to the public".
Ukrainian news outlet, UNN, reported the hack sent fake alerts of a nuclear threat inside Russia, citing Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian-held territory.
A purported screenshot of the fake alert, shared by Atesh on Telegram, warned users that "nuclear warheads mounted on P1-Suns [a Ukrainian attack drone] had been launched at all regions of Russia".
The alert, which included profanities, opened with a message telling residents there was a "risk of getting lively" and told them to "stock up urgently on food for three weeks and hide".
In a statement later, the Russian emergencies ministry said specialists were still working to restore normal operations of the app but that the hack did not impact the country's overall alert system.
It said citizens were informed of alerts through multiple channels including sirens and loudspeakers, text messages, and TV and radio broadcasts, and that the app was "only an additional, ancillary news service".
"The hacking of the mobile app has not had, and cannot have, any impact on the operation of the public alert system," it said on its Telegram channel.
The alerts occurred just minutes before the end of a localised ceasefire in Ukraine's front-line Kherson region , which was implemented last Tuesday and officially ended at 23:00 Sunday.
Fighting had continued elsewhere while the Kherson ceasefire was in place, to allow civilians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky .
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Average daily token calls exceed 175 trillion, government-backed report says, indicating growing demand for AI services
For the first time, the amount of inference data generated by artificial intelligence systems in China has surpassed the amount of data used to train those systems, according to a new government-backed report, illustrating how the country is increasingly adopting AI at scale.
The report released on Saturday by the China Centre for Information Industry Development (CCID), which operates under China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), cited recent official data showing that China’s average daily token calls exceeded 175 trillion, an increase of more than 1,000 times from early 2024.
Inference refers to the process of running trained AI models to respond to user requests, which involves processing units of data known as tokens. As AI adoption accelerates, the volume of token calls, which refers to AI usage through public cloud service providers, provides an indication of growing demand for AI services.

articles.title_orig: Zelensky Ready to Meet Putin in Turkey but Rejects Donbas Handover and Crimea Recognition
articles.title_zh: Zelensky Ready to Meet Putin in Turkey but Rejects Donbas Handover and Crimea Recognition
articles.content_orig:
In brief: Zelensky said he was ready to meet Putin in Turkey to discuss a ceasefire, security guarantees, and occupied territories, but ruled out handing over the Donbas or recognizing Crimea as Russian. He also said Ukraine must be included in any negotiations on ending the war.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said he was ready to meet Russian leader Vladimir Putin in Turkey, expressing hope that Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan could help arrange the talks.
In an interview with CNN Türk , Zelensky described direct negotiations at the presidential level as necessary, arguing that previous contacts between the two sides had failed to end Russia’s war against Ukraine .
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“We are ready for this meeting in Turkey. I know that President Erdoğan has his own ties with Putin. That is why we support holding a meeting in Turkey,” Zelensky said.
He argued that a face-to-face meeting could help resolve issues that have remained unsettled in negotiations between the countries’ delegations and technical working groups.
“That is precisely why I want to meet with him – as the person who makes the decisions,” Zelensky said.
He said a ceasefire along the front line and a mechanism to monitor compliance with any agreements should be among the main topics of a potential meeting.
He also said the leaders should discuss security guarantees, Ukraine’s reconstruction and the status of occupied territories. However, Zelensky ruled out accepting Putin’s demands that Ukraine hand over the Donbas or recognize Crimea as Russian territory, saying such concessions would violate the Ukrainian Constitution.
Zelensky also addressed the possibility of attending the G20 leaders’ summit in Miami in December, saying Ukraine had not yet received an official invitation from Washington.
He said there had been signals that US President Donald Trump might invite Ukraine, potentially alongside an initiative aimed at ending the war.
“The discussion touched upon the possibility that President Trump might invite us to the G20 summit and perhaps put forward an initiative aimed at ending the war. Naturally, if Trump extends an official invitation, we will welcome it,” Zelensky said.
The US invited Putin to the summit in September, raising the possibility of a meeting between the Russian leader and Trump. The Kremlin had previously rejected Zelensky’s proposal to meet Putin on the sidelines of the gathering.
On Saturday, Oct. 31, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington might invite Zelensky if his participation could help produce positive results. Trump also did not rule out the possibility on Nov. 1.
Zelensky stressed that any negotiations over ending the war must include Ukraine, rejecting the idea that other countries could decide its future without Kyiv’s involvement.
“It is impossible. You cannot decide Ukraine’s fate without Ukraine. That would be unfair and would lead nowhere. It is illogical to negotiate the fate of a country without the country itself being present,” he said.
He added that similar attempts by other leaders in the past had failed to produce results.
Zelensky also pointed to Russia’s failure to achieve its initial military objectives, despite its claims that it could conquer Ukraine within days.
“Russia, for instance, considered itself a great power and claimed it would conquer Ukraine in three days. We are now entering the fifth year of the war. For five years, Russia has been unable to conquer Ukraine,” he said.
He added that no third country had the right to negotiate matters of Ukrainian sovereignty without Ukraine’s direct participation.

articles.title_orig: Gulf States Fear Fiercer Iran Retaliation If US Strikes
articles.title_zh: Gulf States Fear Fiercer Iran Retaliation If US Strikes
articles.content_orig:
Third day of indirect talks as Qatar tries to negotiate release of $6bn in Iranian assets that could lead to waterway’s reopening
Officials from the Gulf states are “braced for the worst” as they wait for Washington’s response to an Iranian proposal that could reopen the strait of Hormuz before the US midterm elections on Tuesday.
Indirect talks in Doha ran into a third day on Sunday with Qatar trying to negotiate the release of more than $6bn in Iranian assets, which could lead to the reopening of the strait of Hormuz and the restart of negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme.
The United Arab Emirates envoy Anwar Gargash said another round of escalation was not in the interests of Iran or any of its neighbours. He said: “We are also, as we have shown before, braced for the worst.”
He added: “Relations with Iran are essential, because Iran is our neighbour and we do not want to see it get caught up in a prolonged crisis.”
Qatar’s mediation continued despite unidentified missiles striking a Pakistan-bound Qatari LNG tanker near the strait of Hormuz on Friday. The attack came despite the ship receiving direct clearance and safe-passage approval from Tehran just hours earlier.
In a bid to overcome the lack of trust on both sides, Qatar has been focusing its efforts on reaching an agreement for a plan to compress the process by which the US lifts sanctions and then Iran reopens the strait of Hormuz and starts nuclear talks. Iran has agreed to cut the timetable from seven to two days.
Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said he hoped the US would choose “diplomacy over other paths”. He said Iran was ready for both defence and diplomacy, depending on Washington’s “rationality”. Araghchi said there were currently no plans for direct talks with Washington.
Araghchi has not been attending the mediation in Doha and is due to go to Turkmenistan on Monday, but other Iranian diplomats are heavily involved.
Donald Trump said on Saturday the US had knocked out much of Iran’s military but still had to “take care of” one or two targets, as Tehran warned of reprisals if attacked. He maintained that negotiations with Iran to end the war, started by the US and Israel in February, were “going fine but you know they’re not very reliable”.
Earlier on Saturday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the US was open to a diplomatic solution, while Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, disclosed that he had received a letter from the US vice-president, JD Vance, seeking to revive talks.
Rezaei noted what he described as a positive change in “tone” from the US side but said he had yet to respond.
Speaking to Al Jazeera on Saturday, Araghchi said Iran had offered to open the strait of Hormuz within two days of the US acting to lift the blockade on oil ships, stop blocking the release of Iranian assets and end sanctions on Iranian oil exports.
Ali Nikzad, the deputy speaker of Iran’s parliament, once again signalled that Tehran would be unwilling to discuss its nuclear programme, saying: “Our enemies must understand that the Iranian nation has made a decision not to negotiate on the nuclear issue under any circumstances or under any pressure. This great nation gave its enemies enough opportunity to negotiate in this area, but was faced with repeated breaches of promises and illegal bombing of part of peaceful nuclear facilities.”
Rezaei claimed Trump was being hounded by a war that he claimed was having wider international repercussions than the Vietnam war. He told Iranian TV on Saturday: “Today, wherever Trump goes, he must answer why he started the war against Iran. There is no family in America that has not endured the pressure caused by the war in Iran.”

articles.title_orig: As Europe's right advances, Germany's AfD rethinks its anti-euro roots
articles.title_zh: As Europe's right advances, Germany's AfD rethinks its anti-euro roots
articles.content_orig:
In its new strategy, Germany’s Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is shifting its focus from the country leaving the European Union and the eurozone to reforming the bloc from within. TimesLIVE reports .
The party was founded in 2013 amid dissatisfaction with aid programmes for highly indebted eurozone states. Initially, the AfD opposed the single currency and later extended its criticism to the EU. It gained its greatest support through its tough stance on immigration. Opponents and Germany’s domestic intelligence service say some of the party’s approaches come dangerously close to ideas of the superiority of some groups over others and xenophobia; the AfD rejects accusations of extremism.
Last month, AfD co-leader Alice Weidel presented the “New Course for Europe” strategy at the European Parliament in Strasbourg. It was presented together with allies from the Europe of Sovereign Nations group. The document shifts attention from leaving the eurozone and the EU to revising treaties in order to create a less closely integrated union.
The proposals include a mechanism allowing states to opt out of certain common policies, including in the areas of defence spending and immigration, as well as stricter compliance with budget rules. The strategy leaves open the possibility of retaining the euro. If attempts to reform the EU do not produce results, the question of Germany’s future European course is proposed to be put to a referendum.
More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram .
The issue of abandoning the euro remains controversial for the AfD. Jean-Pascal Hohm, head of the party’s youth wing, Generation Deutschland, believes that a hard anti-European stance could complicate future cooperation with Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union, which currently rejects an alliance with the AfD.
Hohm also tried to pass a resolution at the party congress in August on the youth wing’s commitment to the European idea, but it was withdrawn because of insufficient support. According to him, the issue of the euro proved more controversial within the party than the initiators had expected.
After its historic victory in regional elections in Saxony-Anhalt in September, the AfD, which the article describes as the most popular party in nationwide polls, appears closer to entering the federal government by the end of the decade.
