articles.title_orig: New VOLTA Infostealer Uses Claude, Gemini, and Kimi AI to Rank Victims by Financial Value
articles.title_zh: New VOLTA Infostealer Uses Claude, Gemini, and Kimi AI to Rank Victims by Financial Value
articles.content_orig:
Cybersecurity researchers have discovered a new Windows infostealer malware called VOLTA-AUTODOXER (aka VOLTA) that makes use of a large language model (LLM) to rank a victim's stolen data by their monetization value.
Like other typical stealer families, VOLTA is equipped to harvest passwords and cookies from Chromium-based web browsers; data from Outlook profiles and Slack workspaces; payment cards; cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases; Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions; Microsoft OAuth tokens; SSH and cloud-provider keys; Wi-Fi profiles; and screenshots.
"VOLTA builds a structured evidence bundle about the person behind the machine," Cisco Talos researcher Ryan Fetterman said . "This bundle contains geolocation and home address, employer and employer domain, inferred birth year, card last-4 digits, Slack workspaces, document authorship metadata, iPhone backup indicators, and a live Roblox account valuation."
To make this information more valuable, the malware uses stolen session access to search the victim's Gmail account for receipts to corroborate the home address by extracting emails related to Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart, and PayPal.
Once the necessary information is collected, the bundle is serialized and fed into an artificial intelligence (AI) system for analysis using OpenRouter, a unified LLM API gateway and routing service, along with a system prompt. The requests are defaulted to Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6, failing which it falls back to Moonshot AI's Kimi K2 and Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash.
"VOLTA uses a multi-model architecture to fall back resiliently if it hits a model's refusal, checking each response for phrases like 'I can't' or 'I'm not able,' before passing on to a chain of up to three models," Talos said.
VOLTA features a 240-word system prompt that instructs the model to assume the role of a "forensic intelligence analyst" responsible for drafting a target assessment based on data from a structured evidence bundle. "The bundle is the ONLY permissible source of facts; your training knowledge must never supply a fact about the subject," reads a line from the prompt.
"The required output includes a section titled 'WHAT THEY'RE WORTH' with valuables ranked by monetization with a low/medium/high tier, and a section on 'THEIR OPSEC' containing an assessment of the victim's security posture and password hygiene," Talos explained.
"The model is the operator's triage analyst; it turns a raw credential log into a prioritized and citation-backed dossier of the victim and their monetizable assets."
Data exfiltration happens over Telegram at three different stages -
What's more, VOLTA makes use of a template containing six slots that are filled in at build time. This includes the  Telegram channel used for data exfiltration, API keys, and other settings.
This approach suggests that the malware author is likely either advertising a builder kit to prospective customers or operating it as a bespoke tool under their control to compile a custom binary for each order.
"If VOLTA is indeed a commoditized malware, then the AI dossier capability isn't something the author invented for their own operations," Talos said. "It is a feature which enables a customer of any level of sophistication to point it at victims and start receiving ranked target assessments in their Telegram inbox."
"VOLTA is a mature stealer with a late-stage AI layer added for one purpose: relieving the operator of analytical work. The axis of AI improvement here is not speed or scale but effort displacement."
The disclosure comes as adversarial adoption of generative AI (aka GenAI) is quickly becoming the new normal, as threat actors incorporate the technology into their workflows to develop custom tools or find valuable data, thereby increasing the likelihood of success of their attacks.
"GenAI technologies are also well suited to examine massive amounts of data for the purposes of classification or content searching," Zscaler ThreatLabz said . "Once an attacker has access to the victim’s system, GenAI can therefore be used to search all materials to which a victim's system has access, seeking the most valuable or sensitive data for theft or encryption during the next phase of the attack."
A ransomware actor can leverage this method to identify and acquire the most sensitive data from a compromised network, maximizing the chances that the victim will pay up.
Last week, Talos also detailed an AI-enabled framework called NIK C2 that gives attackers remote access, credential theft, keylogging, defense evasion, surveillance, and ransomware capabilities, while integrating an OpenAI client to send stolen data for AI analysis within the compromised session.
A Go-based, Windows remote access tool, NIK C2 grants persistent control over compromised hosts and supports over 52 commands sent by a command-and-control (C2) server to collect a wide range of data.
The OpenAI integration is notable for the fact that the threat actor can abuse a victim's own OpenAI API key to execute the AI-driven analysis. Specifically, the plant checks if the actor has supplied an API key. In the absence of one, it scans the victim's environment variables for the string "OPENAI_API_KEY" and uses it.
This is a form of LLMjacking, where bad actors steal access to another party's AI model to run their own operations – in this case, against the victim itself – while the legitimate owner pays for the computing power. In addition, it allows the attacker to evade detection by obscuring who made the requests.
"This fallback is not a backup mechanism for API key resolution. It is a deliberate design with significant operational implications," Talos said . "If the victim has configured an OpenAI account on their machine, that account's API key will be used to fund the actor's AI inference."
"NIK C2 reshapes adversary tradecraft by collapsing collection and exploitation into a single continuous session, effectively erasing the offline processing delays that historically granted defenders critical detection windows," Talos said.

articles.title_zh: U.S. crude falls more than 3% amid reports of U.S.-Iran diplomatic efforts
articles.content_orig:
Oil prices fell sharply early on Monday amid reports that both the U.S. and Iran are seeking diplomatic options to bring an end to the Middle East conflict.
Futures for international benchmark Brent crude for January delivery fell 3.91% to $109.00 a barrel as of 4:07 a.m. ET. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for December declined 4.1% to $99.85 per barrel.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that President Donald Trump prefers not to use military force and would like to resolve the Iranian war "diplomatically."
Trump "hasn't made a decision...what the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it, and we really we have everything we need to be successful. But we would prefer to do it peacefully," Rubio said, speaking to reporters over the weekend.
Iranian authorities also signaled that a deal is still possible, following two days of talks mediated by Qatar, as long as demands are implemented tangibly, according to Al Jazeera.
The news come following reports that both the U.S. and Iran are preparing for more military strikes after the midterm elections.
Reports from The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times indicate that the U.S. is preparing for possible renewed military actions after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei on Saturday called for Tehran's armed forces to meet "any level or type of threat" with "an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."
Concerns over the Middle East and Ukraine conflicts will likely linger in the near term.
"Attacks on ships and refineries in the Middle East and on civilians in Ukraine continue, doing little to inspire confidence in the prospects for lasting ceasefires in the foreseeable future," said Tamas Varga, analyst at PVM Oil Associates.
"Nonetheless, hope springs eternal," Varga added.
—CNBC's Lim Hui Jie contributed to this report.

Moscow says a "massive cyber-attack" has affected its app but insists its wider alert system is "operating as normal" . A Ukrainian espionage group claims the messages included fake warnings of nuclear strikes inside Russia
This comes shortly after Ukraine's air raid warning app sent out false warnings of a radiation threat in Kyiv , following an apparent hack

The alerts in Ukraine were sent out just minutes before the end of a localised ceasefire in the front-line Kherson region, our Ukraine reporter Abdujalil Abdurasulov writes

While we wait for further information on the apparent cyber attacks in Russia and Ukraine, here's the latest on the strikes that were reported overnight.
In a statement on Telegram, Russia's Ministry of Defence says it struck a Ukrainian military cargo vessel at sea 58km south of Odesa overnight.
It says the vessel was "delivering cargo intended for the Ukrainian Armed Forces".
Another strike hit a storage site for Ukrainian missile launch systems in the Odesa village of Tuzly, it says.
Meanwhile, a Telegram channel for the city of Odesa says four people were injured in strikes in Odesa overnight. "All received prompt medical assistance," the update says.
It adds that two private homes, a garage and city infrastructure also sustained "significant damage".
The false alerts started at approximately 22:47 (20:47 GMT) on Sunday, with red-level air raids apparently issued nationwide, in Ukrainian.
Additional warnings were issued in Kyiv, with the first reading: "Radiation threat. Radiation threat declared in Kyiv."
The next message, written in Russian, came at 22:48 , which read: "Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across Ukraine. Don't worry, it's Oreshnik flying". Oreshnik is the name of a Russian intermediate-range ballistic missile capable of carrying nuclear or conventional warheads.
A third alert, at 22:49 , again in Ukrainian, said "Chemical threat. There is a threat of a chemical attack on Kyiv. Don't go outside."
At 22:49 , a fourth alert stated there was a "street fighting threat. Street fighting is taking place in Kyiv. Don't go outside."
At 23:53 a series of all clear messages were then delivered to users' phones, which were connected to each of the previous Kyiv alerts, individually declaring each threat clear.
We don't know much about the alerts sent out in Russia. But as we reported earlier, a Ukrainian espionage group claimed fake warnings of nuclear strikes inside Russia had been sent to users.
Dan Johnson Ukraine correspondent, reporting from Kyiv

The warnings were followed by all clear messages just over an hour later.

Oleksander Merezhko, chair of the Ukrainian parliament's foreign affairs committee, has told the BBC the attack did not cause panic or extreme reactions.
Merezhko says Ukrainians, especially in Kyiv, are used to "practically non-stop alerts".
"Secondly, this message was in Russian language which immediately aroused suspicions," he says.

Russia and Ukraine have also exchanged strikes targeting each other's energy infrastructure.

The governor of Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region - home to the Kstovo plant - described a "massive" drone attack during the night and morning.

Some connections were restored on Sunday.

(Kitco NewsWire) - Spot gold and silver prices were sharply lower in late U.S. trading Friday, as a technology-led equity market selloff intensified liquidation pressure across precious metals, offsetting the support normally provided by falling Treasury yields and heightened geopolitical uncertainty. Crude oil prices climbed more than 2% following another tanker attack in the Strait of Hormuz, adding to inflation concerns and expectations that Federal Reserve monetary policy will remain restrictive. Spot gold was trading near $3,879.90 an ounce, down $141.60, or 3.52%, while spot silver was trading near $49.015, down $3.150, or 6.06%, on the session.
Friday's U.S. economic reports presented a mixed picture of moderating wage growth and weakening regional manufacturing activity. The employment cost index increased 0.8% in the third quarter, matching expectations and slowing from 0.9% in the second quarter. The October Chicago purchasing managers' index declined to 55.3 from 58.8 in September, missing expectations near 56.1 but remaining above the 50-point threshold separating expansion from contraction. Friday's softer wage and manufacturing readings followed Thursday's stronger-than-expected third-quarter gross domestic product report, which showed the U.S. economy expanding at a 3.4% annualized pace , compared with 2.2% in the second quarter. September headline personal consumption expenditures inflation accelerated to 3.6% annually, while core PCE inflation increased to 3.1%, reinforcing concerns about persistent underlying price pressure.
Market positioning remains divided between resilient economic growth, persistent inflation and the growing risk of financial-market instability. The Federal Reserve left its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4.00% Wednesday , with two policymakers favoring an immediate 25-basis-point increase. Interest rate futures continued to reflect substantial expectations for further tightening in December, although Friday's moderating employment costs and sharp equity-market decline provided counterweights to the inflationary implications of strong GDP growth and higher energy prices. Treasury yields fell as investors sought the relative safety of government bonds, with the benchmark 10-year yield retreating toward 4.93% and the two-year yield approaching 4.58%. However, gold continued to decline, suggesting that forced liquidation, portfolio rebalancing and the broader outlook for restrictive monetary policy outweighed immediate safe-haven demand.
The Strait of Hormuz and U.S.-Iran situation remained a major source of energy-market uncertainty Friday after another commercial tanker was attacked in the strategic waterway. The vessel was struck by explosive devices attached to its hull by a small boat, highlighting the continuing vulnerability of commercial shipping despite regional diplomatic efforts aimed at reducing tensions. Responsibility for the attack had not been established. The incident intensified concerns that renewed military confrontation involving Iran and the United States could further disrupt Middle Eastern energy exports, particularly as markets assessed the possibility of additional military action following the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections. Negotiations involving Washington, Tehran and regional mediators have yet to produce a confirmed settlement, leaving disagreements over sanctions, maritime security and the future of commercial access through Hormuz unresolved.
Crude oil futures rose more than 2% Friday, reaching their highest settlements since late April as traders assessed the possibility of renewed disruptions to Gulf energy supplies. December Brent crude futures gained $2.76, or 2.4%, to settle at $117.64 a barrel after reaching $118.00 intraday. The more actively traded January Brent contract advanced $2.63 to $113.43, while Nymex WTI futures increased $2.12, or 2.08%, to settle at $104.12. Brent gained approximately 13.6% during October, while WTI rose 15.2%, reflecting persistent concerns about Middle Eastern supply security and the inflationary consequences of the regional conflict.
For gold, the latest Hormuz attack reinforced underlying geopolitical demand, but higher crude prices also heightened the risk that inflation will remain persistent and the Federal Reserve will maintain restrictive monetary policy. The sharp decline in bullion despite falling Treasury yields indicates that broader financial-market liquidation was the more immediate influence on Friday's trading. Silver suffered considerably greater losses as weakness in precious metals coincided with concerns about industrial demand, equity-market valuations and restrictive financing conditions. The widening gold-silver ratio reflected silver's greater sensitivity to deteriorating risk sentiment and concerns about manufacturing activity.
North American equity markets finished sharply lower Friday as disappointing corporate earnings and concerns about artificial intelligence-related investment triggered heavy selling in technology shares. The Dow Jones Industrial Average declined approximately 1.1% to close at 51,770.31, while the S&P 500 fell 1.8% to 7,580.07, its largest daily decline since June. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.9% to finish near 25,437, as weakness in semiconductor and major technology shares dominated trading. Intel plunged nearly 29% following disappointing profit guidance, while concerns surrounding Amazon's capital spending added to pressure on the technology sector. The Russell 2000 declined 1.7% to 2,811.84, indicating that selling extended beyond large-cap growth companies. Canada's S&P/TSX Composite Index also fell sharply, losing more than 2% as weakness in precious metals mining and other resource shares compounded the broader deterioration in risk sentiment.
European equity markets closed mostly lower Friday as technology-sector weakness and concerns about elevated energy prices weighed on investor sentiment. The pan-European Stoxx 600 declined approximately 0.4% to 646.73, while Germany's DAX lost 0.9% to finish near 25,819. France's CAC 40 slipped 0.1% to approximately 7,962, while the U.K.'s FTSE 100 outperformed, advancing 0.1% to around 10,736. The Euro Stoxx 50 fell approximately 1.2%, reflecting heavier losses among major continental companies. European technology shares were particularly weak as the U.S. semiconductor selloff affected global valuations, while higher crude prices added to concerns about inflation, corporate margins and the outlook for regional monetary policy. Despite Friday's losses, the Stoxx 600 finished October higher, reflecting gains earlier in the month.
The key outside markets see Nymex WTI crude oil futures higher and settling at $104.12 a barrel, while December Brent crude futures finished at $117.64. The yield on the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury note declined toward the 4.93% area as demand for government bonds increased during the equity selloff. The U.S. dollar was comparatively firm, supported by defensive demand and expectations for restrictive Federal Reserve policy. However, gold continued to decline, suggesting that forced liquidation, portfolio rebalancing and the broader outlook for restrictive monetary policy outweighed immediate safe-haven demand.
The Strait of Hormuz and U.S.-Iran situation remained a major source of energy-market uncertainty Friday after another commercial tanker was attacked in the strategic waterway. The vessel was struck by explosive devices attached to its hull by a small boat, highlighting the continuing vulnerability of commercial shipping despite regional diplomatic efforts aimed at reducing tensions. Responsibility for the attack had not been established. The incident intensified concerns that renewed military confrontation involving Iran and the United States could further disrupt Middle Eastern energy exports, particularly as markets assessed the possibility of additional military action following the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections. Negotiations involving Washington, Tehran and regional mediators have yet to produce a confirmed settlement, leaving disagreements over sanctions, maritime security and the future of commercial access through Hormuz unresolved.
Crude oil futures rose more than 2% Friday, reaching their highest settlements since late April as traders assessed the possibility of renewed disruptions to Gulf energy supplies. December Brent crude futures gained $2.76, or 2.4%, to settle at $117.64 a barrel after reaching $118.00 intraday. The more actively traded January Brent contract advanced $2.63 to $113.43, while Nymex WTI futures increased $2.12, or 2.08%, to settle at $104.12. Brent gained approximately 13.6% during October, while WTI rose 15.2%, reflecting persistent concerns about Middle Eastern supply security and the inflationary consequences of the regional conflict.
For gold, the latest Hormuz attack reinforced underlying geopolitical demand, but higher crude prices also heightened the risk that inflation will remain persistent and the Federal Reserve will maintain restrictive monetary policy. The sharp decline in bullion despite falling Treasury yields indicates that broader financial-market liquidation was the more immediate influence on Friday's trading. Silver suffered considerably greater losses as weakness in precious metals coincided with concerns about industrial demand, equity-market valuations and restrictive financing conditions. The widening gold-silver ratio reflected silver's greater sensitivity to deteriorating risk sentiment and concerns about manufacturing activity.
North American equity markets finished sharply lower Friday as disappointing corporate earnings and concerns about artificial intelligence-related investment triggered heavy selling in technology shares. The Dow Jones Industrial Average declined approximately 1.1% to close at 51,770.31, while the S&P 500 fell 1.8% to 7,580.07, its largest daily decline since June. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.9% to finish near 25,437, as weakness in semiconductor and major technology shares dominated trading. Intel plunged nearly 29% following disappointing profit guidance, while concerns surrounding Amazon's capital spending added to pressure on the technology sector. The Russell 2000 declined 1.7% to 2,811.84, indicating that selling extended beyond large-cap growth companies. Canada's S&P/TSX Composite Index also fell sharply, losing more than 2% as weakness in precious metals mining and other resource shares compounded the broader deterioration in risk sentiment.
European equity markets closed mostly lower Friday as technology-sector weakness and concerns about elevated energy prices weighed on investor sentiment. The pan-European Stoxx 600 declined approximately 0.4% to 646.73, while Germany's DAX lost 0.9% to finish near 25,819. France's CAC 40 slipped 0.1% to approximately 7,962, while the U.K.'s FTSE 100 outperformed, advancing 0.1% to around 10,736. The Euro Stoxx 50 fell approximately 1.2%, reflecting heavier losses among major continental companies. European technology shares were particularly weak as the U.S. semiconductor selloff affected global valuations, while higher crude prices added to concerns about inflation, corporate margins and the outlook for regional monetary policy. Despite Friday's losses, the Stoxx 600 finished October higher, reflecting gains earlier in the month.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said President Donald Trump would like to resolve the Iranian war "diplomatically," and prefers not to use military force.
Speaking over the weekend, Rubio told reporters that "He [Trump] hasn't made a decision...what the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it, and we really we have everything we need to be successful. But we would prefer to do it peacefully."
The remarks come as reports suggest both sides are gearing up for additional military strikes after the midterm elections.
On Saturday, Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei called for Tehran's armed forces to meet "any level or type of threat" with "an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."
He also ordered that its military database be updated so that "all kinds of physical and non-physical assets of the U.S.-Zionist enemy are brought within the reach of the Armed Forces," referring to U.S. and Israeli forces.
Washington has not explicitly stated it plans to resume attacks on Iran, but reports from The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times indicate the U.S. is preparing for possible renewed military actions after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
On Sunday, Trump told the Right Side Broadcasting Network. "We've had such a victory, and we'll put it away very soon, one way or the other."
"Either they'll make a deal, or we'll just end it," he added.
On Sunday, Iran's foreign ministry designated the U.K.'s Military Intelligence Services as a "hostile group" and accused the Royal Navy and Air Force of supporting "terrorist organizations." In a Telegram post , the ministry said that the move was a response to what it called London's "malicious" actions, including the designation of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as a "terrorist organization."
Tehran has separately accused the U.K. of participating in the U.S.-Iran war by allowing American forces access to British military and logistical bases.
The U.K. had allowed U.S. forces to use RAF Fairford and Diego Garcia for what were described as "defensive" strikes on Iran, according to the BBC.

articles.title_orig: King to address slavery in Antigua as PM says he is open to possible UK apology
articles.title_zh: King to address slavery in Antigua as PM says he is open to possible UK apology
articles.content_orig:
King Charles III is to speak with "unflinching honesty" and "sincere sorrow" on the lasting pain of the transatlantic slave trade during the final leg of his Caribbean tour in Antigua, Buckingham Palace has said.
The King will address Commonwealth leaders on Tuesday in a speech that will touch on the issue.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham earlier wrote in the Guardian that he was "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in slavery - a change in the government's stance.
It is understood the Palace was told in advance of Burnham's comments in an opinion piece on Friday night, and that the King has not made any changes to his speech in light of them.
The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations.
Burnham has previously stuck with the policy of his predecessors and stopped short of offering any consideration of reparation payments.
In an address to the nation to mark Antigua and Barbuda's independence day, Prime Minister Gaston Browne said the history of slavery was painful and "its consequences have not disappeared with the passage of time".
He said the country's pursuit of reparatory justice deserved "seriousness, sensitivity and sustained international engagement".
Browne went on to say that his government was having these conversations in bilateral discussions with the UK and other Commonwealth countries at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM).
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch described "endless talk about apologies" as a "distraction" from solving current problems.
She told BBC Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: "The transatlantic slave trade happened centuries ago. It is time for the Commonwealth to start looking forwards, not endlessly backwards."
The King will make his speech at the CHOGM.
He "will not shy away from confronting the most shameful aspects of the past during this visit", a Palace spokesperson said.
"You may therefore expect him to address them in his speech with unflinching honesty, sincere sorrow and respect for the wider discussions that will be taking place between relevant governments on this issue at CHOGM and beyond."
When asked about the King's reaction to the prime minister's comments, the spokesperson said it would "not be appropriate" for the King to address matters of policy relating to the government's position.
The Caribbean tour has again thrust the King into the difficult debates over the UK's colonial legacy in the region.
On his first stop in the Bahamas, the King delivered a speech in which he spoke of the "suffering of the past".
In Guyana, he visited the site of a Slave Rebellion , where hundreds of enslaved people were killed.
Buckingham Palace said it was a moment for the King to learn more about the history of slavery and resistance. His engagements have also covered the environment, opportunities for young people and trade relationships with the UK.
Royal sources have stressed that the decisions around making an apology were a matter for government, not the Palace.
"His Majesty is well practised on the diplomatic tightrope," a Royal aide said. "He is up for challenging visits with complex issues and relationships in play. He sees it as his role to bat for Britain, the Realms and wider Commonwealth."
In a piece for the Guardian published on Friday night, Burnham described the transatlantic slave trade as a "brutal and barbaric violation", and said Britain "must face up to the past".
His separate pledge in his article to strengthen the work of the Commonwealth as an organisation will be welcomed by the King, who views the collection of 56 countries as a powerful vehicle for change.
The King will be giving the opening speech at CHOGM, which gathers leaders from those 56 states every two years in a different part of the Commonwealth.
The biennial meeting's official theme this year is Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth.
Queen Camilla is with the King in Antigua and, as the couple attended a church service on Sunday morning ahead of joining celebrations to mark Independence Day on the island, there was a reminder of what the intended focus of the week will be.
Bishop of North Eastern Caribbean and Aruba, Ernest Flemming, told the congregation the "prosperity" of the Commonwealth must be a "shared prosperity".
"True partnership requires mutual respect, it requires listening, it requires fairness."
A Buckingham Palace spokesperson said: "Institutions are under strain across the globe. The Commonwealth has scale and breadth, but is also small enough for leaders to know each other and co-operate together."
The King, they said, "contributes ideas and encouragement on a wide range of issues, delivering practical results which help improve the lives of millions".
Later on Sunday, the King was left drenched and without an umbrella when a torrential downpour interrupted an Independence Day ceremony.
The Queen was swiftly given an umbrella when the rain started, while the King was seen gesturing to be given one of his own.
It has been a difficult few months for the King, with developments surrounding his brother, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor , and the publication of a book by his former brother-in-law, Earl Spencer.
In addition, his son, the Duke of Sussex, made a surprise move back to the UK with his wife Meghan and their two children in August.
Asked whether the King was confident that his approach to family matters had been the right one in terms of public attitudes towards the institution, the response was concise. "Yes," a senior aide told the BBC. "That is why he takes the actions he does - and has done."
On the serious allegations that have emerged about Meghan's father , Thomas Markle, the Palace did not want to get involved publicly: "We wouldn't comment on private family matters."
The King is also still being treated for cancer. He was diagnosed in early 2024 and the Palace says he remains on a "positive trajectory".
In hot and humid conditions, he will soon celebrate his 78th birthday and will have carried out about 36 engagements by the end of this nine-day tour of the Caribbean.

articles.title_zh: Binance sees $3.64 billion in net outflows as withdrawals resume after massive hack
articles.content_orig:
Binance said it recorded $3.64 billion in net outflows after reopening withdrawals on Sunday following a $6.3 billion hack, as customers rushed to move funds off the platform.
The exchange processed $4.65 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits between 6 a.m. and 3:30 p.m. UTC on Nov. 1, Binance said in a post on X.
The resulting net outflows represented 2.1% of Binance's $171 billion in total assets, based on its latest available proof-of-reserves data as of Oct. 28.
Binance said withdrawal volumes had declined and were stabilizing following an initial spike, while deposit volumes remained substantial.
The exchange began restoring withdrawals in phases at 6 a.m. UTC on Sunday, with services resuming across all 15 networks and assets included in the initial phase by 12:36 p.m. UTC. It said testing was continuing for the remaining networks and assets.
Binance founder and former CEO Changpeng Zhao sought to reassure users following the breach, writing on X that "98% choose to stay!" He said most of the net outflows occurred within the first couple of hours after withdrawals resumed. "Trust isn't earned by what you say in good times. It's earned by what you do in hard times," Zhao added.
The withdrawals followed a record $6.3 billion hack of Binance last week. The FBI attributed the attack to North Korean hackers, identifying the operation as TraderTraitor.
The exchange has said it would absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds rather than pass the losses on to users.
Binance said it had covered around 95% of the impacted amount, up from 90% in its previous update. The exchange said the remaining 5% consisted of less liquid tokens that would take longer to source in the quantities required.

Saudi air defenses intercepted one Houthi ballistic missile and one drone launched toward Saudi Arabia’s southern region on November 1. If all had gone according to plan, the United States v Wanzhou Meng and Huawei Technologies would have opened in a federal courtroom in the waning months of President Donald Trump’s first term. And what a trial it would have been: an heir to one of China’s most successful and strategically important companies, detained in Canada and extradited to the U.S., on trial for allegedly lying to banks about Huawei operations in Iran that were in violation of American sanctions on the country. But Xi Jinping forestalled that humiliating spectacle by ordering the arrest of two Canadians in China, Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor, and not releasing them until the U.S. and Canada allowed Meng, the daughter of Huawei’s founder, to return to China in September 2021. Five years later the United States v Huawei Technologies , minus Meng, is finally underway. Noah Berman reports from the courtroom in Brooklyn.
In other articles, Leon Panetta speaks with Bob Davis about his dealings with China as a Congressman, White House Chief-of-Staff, CIA Director and Secretary of Defense.
Noah Berman on DayOne , the Singaporean data center operator that is helping Chinese companies realise their AI ambitions.
In The Big Picture , Savannah Billman writes about the enormous popularity of AI-generated “short dramas” in China.
Lizzi C. Lee and Simon Hedlin on the barriers to a common-sense Sino-U.S. AI safety agreement .
And finally, be sure to catch up on the latest episode of our weekly podcast , with Peiyue Wu talking about her recent cover on dual-use farms in China.
Want this emailed directly to your inbox? Sign up to receive our free newsletter.
In 2021 Meng Wanzhou, daughter of Huawei Technologies founder Ren Zhengfei, signed a “statement of facts” to resolve U.S. charges against her. According to that statement, “Ms. Meng [told HSBC] … Huawei’s relationship with Skycom was ‘normal business cooperation’ and … she described Skycom as a … ‘third party Huawei works with’ in Iran … Those statements were untrue because, as Ms. Meng knew, … Huawei controlled Skycom.” The U.S. let Meng go regardless because the Chinese government made it clear that it would not release two Canadian hostages until she was freed. Five years later the U.S. government’s case against Huawei is finally underway in New York, with Meng safely back in China.
Leon Panetta fought with, and engaged with China over a long career in politics. The former Congressman, White House Chief of Staff, CIA Director and Defense Secretary talks with Bob Davis about why China thinks President Trump is good for China.
“If China senses weakness, they’ll take advantage of it,” Panetta says. “Right now, China is in a stronger position because we’re locked in a war in Iran, our economy is being impacted by that war, and there’s a lot of unpredictability about the U.S. China has been able to take advantage in areas where once we had some influence, particularly in the Pacific.”
Illustration by Lauren Crow
The U.S. government doesn’t want America’s best chips to power Chinese data centers that would then help Chinese companies hone their AI models and applications. DayOne, a Singapore-based data center provider, profits from this by building data centers in Southeast Asia where Chinese AI firms can legally access America’s best chips. Noah Berman looks at DayOne and the IPO prospectus it has just issued. “DayOne’s rise,” he writes, “illustrates how companies can profit, and even gain backing from American investors, as U.S. export controls lead Chinese companies to seek access to data centers overseas.”
Are you, like the Old Dad who writes this newsletter, also a parent who dreads the short videos on YouTube and elsewhere that so easily reel in your kids? Alas, writes Savannah Billman , if China is anything to go by — as it increasingly is when it comes to tech trends — the madness is only going to get worse. Almost 900 million (!) Chinese people are watching AI-generated “short dramas”, issued as a seemingly endless stream of two-minute videos, on a new generation of apps tailored to the new genre. Over the first half of this year alone about 267,000 AI short videos were released. Ugh.
Recent steps taken towards the establishment of a U.S.-China AI incident-reporting channel are important, write Lizzi C. Lee and Simon Hedlin . But, they add, there is “a more pressing issue: frontier AI companies currently do not provide the information they need”.

articles.title_orig: AI investors hedge against losses amid tech stock selloff
articles.title_zh: AI investors hedge against losses amid tech stock selloff
articles.content_orig:
Investor enthusiasm for artificial intelligence's potential to transform the global economy has fueled massive bets on the sector; however, growing concerns about a possible downturn are prompting investors to seek financial protection against losses, The Wall Street Journal reported Saturday.
“We’re seeing really significant demand from folks looking to protect downside,” said Stephen Solaka, a senior vice president at Gateway Investment Advisers.
Investors and technology executives are increasingly turning to financial instruments such as put options and credit-default swaps to protect their investments.
Put options give investors the right to sell shares at a predetermined price before a specified date. For shareholders seeking protection, these contracts can limit potential losses if stock prices fall sharply, although investors must pay a premium for that protection.
A combination of rising borrowing costs for major data center projects and chip purchases, falling share prices among AI companies, and a broader stock market selloff has heightened concerns about the sector's financial outlook.
Friday's technology stock selloff wiped out more than $1 trillion in market value. The Nasdaq 100 index fell 3.4%, while the broader S&P 500 dropped 1.8%. The S&P 500's technology sector was hit particularly hard, declining more than 4.2%, NBC News reported Friday.
The growing demand for financial protection comes as AI companies continue seeking enormous amounts of capital to fund infrastructure development and expansion.
According to Solaka, some investors have accumulated such substantial gains from technology stocks that they now prioritize protecting their wealth over pursuing further returns.
“These people have made so much money, they’re quitting to hedge their stock,” Solaka said, adding that some companies restrict employees’ trades.
For example, trading in put options tied to AI cloud infrastructure company CoreWeave surged to record levels in October and remained elevated, according to data from Cboe Global Markets.
Investors are also turning to credit-default swaps, financial contracts that protect against a borrower failing to repay its debt.
According to the report, the cost of insuring against debt defaults by major technology companies, including Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, and Oracle, rose over the past month to its highest level since 2021.
“There were no exceptions, suggesting broad market concern about the sector rather than idiosyncratic credit events at individual companies,” said Eugene Grinberg, a co-founder of bond data provider Solve.
As investment in AI infrastructure grows, trading firm Jump Trading has begun offering financial contracts that allow companies to protect themselves against a potential collapse in the price of computing power.
For example, companies renting out Nvidia chips could use these contracts to lock in a minimum rental price, protecting revenue if demand for AI computing power falls.
The growing demand for financial protection is reminiscent of the events depicted in The Big Short , when investors used credit-default swaps to bet against mortgage-backed securities before the 2008 financial crisis. Unlike those investors, however, many of today's technology shareholders are not necessarily betting on a market collapse, but seeking to protect gains accumulated during the AI boom.

articles.title_zh: Ukraine defies Trump to resume attacks on Russian oil refineries
articles.content_orig:
Kremlin says Kyiv is ‘simply ignoring’ US wishes days before midterm elections after reported strikes on two oil sites
Ukraine has resumed its attacks on Russian oil refineries in defiance of pressure from Donald Trump ahead of the US midterm elections, as a ceasefire in the occupied town of Oleshky ended on Sunday night.
Russian state media said on Sunday Ukrainian long-range drones had set fire to the Kstovo refinery in Nizhny Novgorod oblast overnight, soon after a major strike against another big refinery in Samara oblast, owned by the Russian state energy giant Rosneft.
The Wall Street Journal had reported that Ukraine had given in to pressure from the White House to stop bombing Russian energy infrastructure.
Ukrainian officials, however, told the Kyiv Independent newspaper that they never agreed to a demand from Jared Kushner, the US president’s son-in-law, to pause refinery strikes for 30 days. The raids on Russia restarted on Friday, Kremlin officials said, complaining that Kyiv was now “simply ignoring” US wishes.
Trump has blamed the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy , for the rise in global fuel prices, and last month lifted US sanctions on Russian diesel.
Zelenskyy has not acknowledged the latest refinery attacks, in an apparent attempt to avoid angry US reprisals. Instead, he said his armed forces had hit a defence industry enterprise in Russia’s Rostov region that made missiles. A Pantsir missile system was destroyed, he said, as part of Ukraine’s continuing “long-range sanctions”.
Zelenskyy said his country was obliged to retaliate because of a remorseless campaign by Moscow, using drones and ballistic missiles, against vulnerable city-based energy facilities. Four Ukrainian regions were hit by Russia overnight, with electricity cut as a result in hundreds of thousands of households.
“The intensity of the strikes is very high, and the Russians are seeking to maximally exploit the ​deficit of ballistic missile interceptors,” the Ukrainian president said on Telegram. Kyiv experienced power cuts lasting eight to 10 hours on Sunday after a critical thermal power plant was damaged.
Zelenskyy said Russia was suffering record losses, with 54,400 military personnel killed and wounded in October – the highest monthly figure since the full-scale war began. He said Ukraine recaptured 96.2 sqkm (37 sq miles) of its territory last month, 10.4 sqkm (4 sq miles) more than Moscow managed to seize, and emphasised: “Russia is losing.”
The latest attacks came before a six-day local ceasefire brokered by the US first lady, Melania Trump, came to an end in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky. Hundreds of residents were reunited with their loved ones over the weekend in northern Ukraine, with both sides hailing the evacuation mission as a success.
“The ceasefire, which was in effect from October 27 to November 1, has ended,” said Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, hailing what had been an “important step in our joint humanitarian efforts”.
after newsletter promotion
Ukrainian observers say the Russian military used the truce to reinforce its positions and to swap hungry and exhausted troops garrisoned in Oleshky. The town sits on the left bank of the Dnipro River, to the east, and is opposite the larger city of Kherson, which Ukraine recaptured in autumn 2022. A renewed Russian onslaught is inevitable, the observers believe.
The pope said on Sunday he hoped cooperation between ⁠Russia and Ukraine in implementing the Oleshky ceasefire – the most significant since 2022 – would ⁠pave the ⁠way ​for broader peace efforts.
“I hope that the cooperation between the parties, which made this necessary humanitarian gesture possible, will strengthen their willingness to engage in dialogue,” he said during his Sunday prayer.
Trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the US are likely to take place later this month, and Kremlin officials said on Sunday that Vladimir Putin was willing to talk directly to Zelenskyy by phone. They added that European leaders who support Ukraine should not be involved in any such call.
There is little prospect of a wider breakthrough, however, as the Russian president’s maximalist demands remain unchanged. He is insisting that Ukraine give up all of the eastern Donetsk oblast – which Russia has been unable to seize since 2014 – as well as further territory in Kherson and Zaporizhzhia provinces, which the Kremlin does not control but says it has “annexed”.

articles.title_zh: Inside Xiong'an: How China's "City of the Future" Blends Smart Governance with Sustainable Growth
articles.content_orig:
Par Wan Xiubin, Zheng Hai'ou, Shao Yuzi, People's Daily
Above ground, expansive green spaces blend seamlessly with modern architecture. Beneath the surface, a network spanning more than 100 kilometers links underground utility corridors that deliver water, electricity, gas, heating, and communications.
In the cloud, a digital city is taking shape alongside the physical one, while the Xiong'an Urban Computing Center keeps watch over the entire city. A "city of the future" is steadily taking shape in the Xiong'an New Area, north China's Hebei province.
Rejecting sprawling, haphazard urban expansion, Xiong'an has adopted a different approach, with planning preceding construction, underground infrastructure built before above-ground development, and trees planted before the city takes shape. Modern governance has been integrated into every stage of urban development.
In the Rongdong area, the first developed urban area in Xiong'an, trees flourish and buildings stand in neat rows. There are no tangled overhead power lines, and the roads show no signs of repeated digging and patching.
This stability stems from an extensive underground utility tunnel system connecting parking facilities beneath 95 housing complexes. Using a hybrid of China's BeiDou satellite navigation and 5G indoor positioning, the system maintains reliable signals underground. Smart sensors distributed throughout the tunnels monitor environmental conditions in real time, enabling proactive maintenance. "Traffic flows smoothly both above and below ground. Living here feels safe and convenient," said Zhou Qiang, a local resident.
By prioritizing subsurface infrastructure, Xiong'an has built resilience into its foundation while deploying digital twin technology to create a synchronized virtual environment. Ma Yongjun, head of operations of the infrastructure construction company of China Xiong'an Group, starts each workday by logging into the digital twin system. The system provides a detailed view of the utility tunnels, with real-time updates on temperature, humidity, water pressure, and gas concentrations.
"When a problem arises, the system automatically issues an alert. It can be detected in the cloud and addressed directly inside the utility tunnel," Ma said.
Under clear autumn skies, birds flock to the Yannan dike of Baiyangdian Lake, while the Nanhe water conservancy hub is reflected in the water. The hub links the vast wetlands of Baiyangdian on one side with Xiong'an's modern buildings on the other.
Before the Xiong'an New Area was established, water quality across Baiyangdian was generally below Grade V, the lowest classification in the country's five-tier water quality system. Water flows had declined, and the waterways had become severely fragmented. At the Fuhe River estuary wetland, the gateway to Baiyangdian, polluted upstream water once flowed directly into the lake.
Zhu Baofeng, head of the water conservancy and water environment construction and operations division at China Xiong'an Group Ecological Construction Investment Co., Ltd., led his team in restoring the wetland through nature-based purification techniques, breathing new life into the wetland.
In recent years, Xiong'an has taken an integrated approach to replenishing water supplies, tackling pollution and preventing floods. It has advanced five major initiatives in parallel, including dredging waterways, linking lakes and ponds, restoring wetlands, replenishing water supplies in a science-based manner, and strengthening flood control.
"Baiyangdian has returned to its former vitality!" said Zhang Xuenong, chairman of the Baiyangdian Photographers Association in Anxin county, who has documented the lake's transformation in more than 100,000 photos. In recent years, rare birds such as the Baer's Pochard have frequently appeared in his photographs.
"The city and the lake now complement each other, and every shot captures a beautiful scene," Zhang said.
Water quality in Baiyangdian has remained stable at Grade III for five consecutive years. As of 2026, the number of wild bird species recorded there has risen to 296, up 90 from before the Xiong'an New Area was established. The number of fish species has recovered to 50.
"It feels like living in a garden," said Yuan Yuxin, a resettled resident who moved with his family into Lixian Garden residential community in Rongdong area in 2023.
"There's a supermarket just a few minutes' walk away, and my grandchildren live close to their schools. I play ball at the community senior care center every day. Life is fulfilling and comfortable," Yuan said.
In Nanwenying Community, where Yuan lives, household files document residents' needs and everyday concerns.
"We maintain individual files for each of our more than 3,700 households, covering matters such as health care and elderly care. We update them every two months," said Wang Weixiao, head of the Nanwenying Community.
The records have been organized into more than 80,000 entries and distilled into three lists covering available resources, residents' needs and concerns, and responsibilities. This helps streamline the many tasks involved in community governance, said Wang.
A settled home is the foundation for a fulfilling life. With equitable, high-quality public services, meticulous community-level governance and a thriving industrial base, Xiong'an is helping residents build settled homes and fulfilling lives.
"Governance is not something to be addressed after construction is complete. Xiong'an has integrated planning, construction and governance from the outset, ensuring that urban management is guided by clear rules from the very beginning," said Liu Zhenming, deputy director of the Natural Resources and Planning Bureau of the Xiong'an New Area.

Kombos says Ankara has spent decades violating Cyprus’ sovereignty while invoking the UN Charter against others, calling the gap between Turkey’s ‘words and deeds’ stark.
The Trump State Department denounced the recent eastern Mediterranean maritime agreement between NATO member Turkey and the fractured Libyan state.
The Turkey-Libya deal has also caused frustration and anger among many nations because they say it rewrote the established sea borders of the sensitive Mediterranean Sea region, where large deposits of gas might be located.
The Eastern Libyan parliament approved the maritime accord in mid-October. The region is ruled by military leader Khalifa Haftar, who has formed an alliance with Turkey — the maritime deal ignores Libya’s internationally recognized government in Tripoli in the northwestern part of the oil-rich country.
A U.S. State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital: "The announcement of the ratification of the Turkish-Libyan delimitation memorandum of understanding has raised tensions in the region and is unhelpful and provocative — and our position on this matter has not changed."
BILLION-DOLLAR POWER LINK CONNECTING ISRAEL TO EUROPE HITS ROADBLOCK IN BITTER REGIONAL FEUD
Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan gives a press conference at the NATO summit on June 25, 2025, in The Hague, Netherlands. (Pierre Crom/Getty Images)
The spokesperson added: "We encourage all countries, including partners in the Eastern Mediterranean, to resolve maritime disputes through good-faith negotiations and avoid any provocative behavior. Greece and Türkiye are both NATO allies . We encourage them to engage bilaterally to address any areas of disagreement."
According to the spokesperson, "Peaceful resolution of such disputes opens the way for commercial investment and exploration that will benefit the entire region."
According to the Turkish news agency Anadolu Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan on Wednesday said the maritime agreement between Turkey and Libya was "entirely legitimate" and not in violation of international law.
He added: "This is an entirely legitimate agreement, both from a legal and a political perspective. There is no need to debate it."
Reuters reported Fidan also shot back at critics of the deal. "There are countries reacting to this. We know why they are reacting. Some are doing so because they need to, some really do have strategic problems with this issue. ​ However, this is an entirely legitimate deal, both from a legal and a statutory perspective. ​There is no need to argue this."
NETANYAHU WARNS TURKEY SHOULD NOT GET F-35S, CITING ERDOĞAN'S HOSTILITY TOWARD NATO ALLIES
Libya's military strongman Khalifa Haftar, center, attends a conference for the country's development and reconstruction on Sept 2024. (Khaled Nasraoui/picture-alliance/dpa/AP Images)
Fox News Digital sought comment from both Turkey and Libya but did not get a response by time of publication.
Greek Minister of Foreign Affairs George Gerapetritis angrily wrote on his ministry’s website that, "The memorandum will not be implemented. And it will not be implemented for the simple reason that it produces no legal effects whatsoever, as it is entirely contrary to international law." He added, "Türkiye had established a system of influence in Libya, essentially seeking to advance its own interests" and the Turkish media has ramped up its anti-Greece rhetoric. "There is a constant stream of reports pushing the Turkish government to become even more aggressive."
Endy Zemenides, the executive director of the Hellenic American Leadership Council, told Fox News Digital that the Turkey-Libya agreement "absolutely" endangers the security of the U.S. and its allies.
He said: "This memorandum specifically infringes on U.S. companies and U.S. energy policy. It effectively denies maritime rights and zones of Crete. Crete is NATO’s southernmost base. And the U.S. has been increasingly relied upon because of wars in the Mideast." He noted that the American companies Exxon and Chevron are present in Crete.
US-BACKED ISRAEL-MOROCCO DEAL DEEPENS ABRAHAM ACCORDS AMID GROWING REGIONAL THREATS
A drilling platform is seen from Larnaca port, in the eastern Mediterranean island of Cyprus. (Petros Karadjias, File/AP)
Zemenides said the Turkey-Libya deal is a way of pushing the U.S. out of the region. The U.S. has not been able to rely on Turkey for a decade, said Zemenides. He continued that "allowing Turkey to challenge the pro-Western order" is not good for American interests.
The European Union invoked unusually strong language targeting the deal, declaring it in violation of maritime law.
"The EU position regarding the MoU is firm and clear. As outlined in the European Council Conclusions of December 2019 and reiterated in June 2025, the Türkiye-Libya Memorandum of Understanding infringes upon the sovereign rights of third States and does not comply with the Law of the Sea. It is null and void and cannot produce any legal consequences for third States."

Israel also blasted Turkey and Libya. The Jewish state has developed a troika alliance with both Greece and Cyprus . Israel’s foreign ministry said on X it "strongly condemns the decision of the Libyan House of Representatives to ratify the Maritime Jurisdiction Memorandum between Turkey and Libya."
Israel’s foreign ministry added on X, "This agreement infringes upon the sovereign rights of our close allies in the region. Regretfully, once again we see Turkey working to destabilize the east Mediterranean region."

China’s ruling Communist Party emphasized loyalty in a new resolution aimed at strengthening internal discipline and continuing its anti-corruption efforts. This resolution, discussed at a recent party leadership meeting, calls for enhancing loyalty among members and judging officials based on their commitment to party values, as seen through their work, behavior, and family values.
The resolution acknowledges ongoing problems such as ideological and organizational impurities and aims to address them through an extensive anti-graft campaign that has already affected millions in the bureaucracy. This initiative comes in anticipation of a leadership change where President Xi Jinping is expected to secure another five-year term.
The party plans to improve oversight of officials, including stricter checks on personal disclosures and the financial activities of their families. The anti-corruption campaign will also target hidden forms of graft, including the misuse of technology and financial systems to facilitate corruption.
While promoting collective leadership, the document still reinforces Xi’s authority, urging party members to support him fully in thought and action. Xi emphasized the importance of rigorous self-governance to maintain the party’s integrity and legacy for future generations.

President Donald Trump had a tense exchange with a reporter at his Halloween party at Mar-a-Lago on Saturday night.
The president briefly took questions in the ballroom of his Palm Beach resort , flanked by Secret Service agents and surrounded by partygoers in top hats, feathered headdresses, wings and sparkles.
“Do you expect to go back to war with Iran this week,” a reporter asked the president, who said he came dressed as “Donald Trump.”
“Why would you ask such a stupid question?” Trump snapped back, indicating that the reporter was from The New York Times .
“Let’s say I did, would I tell you? Let's say I didn't, would I tell you?” Trump said, throwing his hands up in the air. “I can’t tell you that…It’s not a question for The New York Times .”
The president has long had a combative relationship with the press , launching personal attacks on reporters, seeking to bar them from the White House and filing multimillion-dollar lawsuits against media outlets. Last month, he berated The Independent ’s Andrew Feinberg in the Oval Office, calling him a “sick person” who “better be careful.”
Speculation has mounted for weeks that Trump, 80, will launch a new offensive against Iran following the midterm elections on Tuesday, which will determine which party controls the House and the Senate.
U.S. officials warned several Gulf allies to prepare for a short, intense military campaign after Election Day as Trump weighs renewed strikes on Iranian infrastructure and nuclear sites, two diplomats briefed on the matter told The Associated Press this week.
The president also reportedly met with top military leaders on Thursday, including Admiral Brad Cooper, the commander of U.S. Central Command.
“We may do another little Epic Fury,” Trump said at a rally on October 23, referring to the U.S.-Israeli bombing campaign this past spring. “Or they’ll agree.”
Eight months into the war, large-scale attacks have largely paused, but the fragile lull has left no clear end to the conflict in sight.
The war has led to the deaths of at least 18 U.S. service members and wounded hundreds more. It has also reportedly cost the U.S. military at least $47 billion and dramatically driven up fuel prices . Multiple polls indicate the war is broadly unpopular.
Polls also suggest that the Republican Party could endure severe losses on Election Day, amid voter frustration over the war and the cost of living, potentially costing them their House and Senate majorities.

articles.title_orig: Israel election: When will government be formed, who will lead it?
articles.title_zh: Israel election: When will government be formed, who will lead it?
articles.content_orig:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has lost his coalition’s parliamentary majority following legislative elections on October 27.
But a bloc of Jewish parties opposing Netanyahu also failed to win a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, leaving Israel without a clear path to a new government.
What’s ahead is likely weeks of political wrangling as Israel’s disparate factions weigh possible governing arrangements, including a unity government bringing rival factions together or a minority government reliant on outside support. If they fail to reach an agreement, Israel could head back to the polls.
Here’s what you should know:
The pro-Netanyahu coalition won 53 seats:
A bloc of Jewish parties opposing Netanyahu won 48 seats:
Arab-led parties won 19 seats:
That leaves all existing blocs short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset, meaning some parties would have to realign or join forces across bloc lines to form a new government.
Israel’s election results must be officially certified and presented to President Isaac Herzog by November 4 .
The new Knesset is scheduled to be sworn in on November 10 .
Herzog must task one incoming Knesset member with forming a new government by November 11 . He is expected to make his decision with input from party leaders, selecting the candidate he believes has the best chance of building a coalition.
The candidate commissioned by Herzog has 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible extension of 14 days .
He has not said yet, but the most likely candidates are Netanyahu or former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot, whose Yashar party received the most votes in the opposition bloc.
According to Israel’s Yedioth Ahronoth media, Eisenkot may have an edge over Netanyahu as some Arab-led parties consider endorsing him in a bid to oust Netanyahu.
Herzog, for his part, has urged Israeli politicians to move away from rigid partisan stances and look for “creative solutions” that will lead to a new government and avoid a second round of elections.
Before the election, Herzog said he would do everything he could to spare the country another election cycle, even if that means pressing for a national unity government that brings together rivals Netanyahu and Eisenkot.
Eisenkot and other opposition leaders have previously ruled out partnering with the Arab-led parties .
Former Prime Minister Ehud Barak, however, has said he believes they “can change their mind”, arguing that Netanyahu would do in their position.
“If Netanyahu had a similar problem, he would immediately invite Mansour Abbas”, the leader of Ra’am and “give him the role of a minister of interior”, Barak told France 24 on Friday.
Abbas himself has signalled a willingness to work the opposition camp, saying Eisenkot’s conditions would not pose an obstacle for his party, according to Israel’s Channel 12.
Yousef Jabareen from the Arab-led Joint List has also said that his party is ready for the “ousting of the Netanyahu government”.
“The change comes through Jewish-Arab partnership, a true and equal partnership,” he wrote on X.
Even if Arab-led parties do not formally join the opposition’s coalition, they could prop it up from outside by helping it pass a confidence vote in the Knesset.
Raluca Ganea, co-founder of Israeli civil society group Zazim, told Al Jazeera that a coalition between the opposition bloc and the Arab-led parties representing the Palestinian citizens of Israel “is the only path forward for Israeli democracy as a whole”.
If Herzog’s first candidate fails to form a government within the 42 days, the Israeli president has the option of asking another Knesset member to try to do so within 28 days. If that candidate also fails, a majority of Knesset members could put forward a third candidate, who would have a final 14 days to try to assemble one.
Even without a coalition commanding at least 61 seats, a candidate could still try to form a minority government by relying on outside support from smaller parties, including Arab-led parties, or negotiate a power-sharing arrangement with alternating prime ministers.
If none of these options succeed and deadlock persists, the Knesset would be formally dissolved, and Israelis would return to the polls for another round of elections.
Those elections would have to be called within 90 days.
Netanyahu stays on as caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed.
If the process drags out, that could leave Israel’s longest-serving prime minister in power for months more, even if he ultimately fails to become part of the next governing coalition.
